subject_of_business_title: Fight against cancer (topical debate)
paragraph: madam president, what makes cancer so dangerous is that it is such a complex disease. tumours that come under the same umbrella are often quite different. there are many different kinds of breast cancer, but they’re still called breast cancer. hodgkin’s lymphoma attacks young lives, not old, and it is 95% curable, which is wonderful. but other cancers are still an automatic death sentence. in addition, genetic instability means that tumours go through an evolutionary process which means they can quickly become resistant to treatments that were working. but we know that one in three cancers might be curable, so we need to do more. advancements in genomic research are allowing research on tumour mutations to move quickly. further studies in epigenetics are allowing researchers to look deeper, beyond dna, and to combine the medical data with critical information about the kind of external and environmental factors that have been mentioned here today. we must seize the opportunities created by these advancements in biomedicine, bioinformatics, big data and artificial intelligence to help us in this fight. so i call on ursula van der leyen to make the fight against cancer an absolute priority of the next commission, in scientific research as well as in the medical area.

subject_of_business_title: Requirements for payment service providers - Measures to strengthen administrative cooperation in order to combat VAT fraud (debate)
paragraph: madam president, first i would like to welcome the commissioner’s commitment that he has just articulated to make vat and tax fraud in general his priority. commissioner, i think you would also have huge support in this house. you mentioned that the numbers of the value added tax gap are slowly and gradually decreasing but, according to the commission estimates and indications, it should still be around eur 130 billion in 2018 and that is indeed still quite a high number. as was also mentioned by other colleagues, the vat carousel frauds, whereby criminals abuse the eu cross—border trading system, contribute eur 50 billion on average per year in lost revenue for member states’ tax authorities. the legislation we are debating here today will help drastically reduce the revenues lost to vat fraud in our financial systems. their losses are damaging not only to the governments. they are also felt throughout the economic chain and therefore damage the vast majority of legitimate businesses, particularly small and medium-sized companies in the european union. i therefore fully support the efforts to address the deficiencies in vat regimes in europe. from the european parliament perspective, we have emphasised the importance of legislation being appropriate for the modern age. this is something we will need to monitor on a continuous basis to ensure that our rules are fit for purpose and achieve the goal of increasing the efficiency of vat collection and combating fraud. we must not forget the time and money it takes, especially for smaller companies, to collect and report their appropriate vat information to authorities. therefore, for our group it is important that the new rules do not add an undue administrative burden which may hamper the efforts of smaller businesses to grow, particularly across borders within the single market. european legislation in this area needs to be future-oriented with a clear focus on ensuring it can be applied as business models evolve in the coming years. i therefore appreciate that the parliament has specifically pointed to the digital arena in this report as our commercial environment becomes ever more digital. i would also encourage vat authorities to consider the development of artificial-intelligence-based solutions to tackle fraud. specifically, artificial intelligence could be used to create a risk model that would help identify anomalies in the system. in this way, the ai could minimise hours spent  by officials in compiling such information. by increasing efficiency, we can target carousel frauds in particular in a more effective manner. let me conclude by thanking the rapporteur and colleagues for their cooperation on these two files. we have drafted two reports that reflect parliament’s priorities, particularly as regards the administrative cooperation and payment service providers. i believe that these are the right steps needed in the area of tax collection, which enhance cross-border cooperation on the one hand and help fight tax fraud on the other.

subject_of_business_title: Automated decision-making processes: Ensuring consumer protection, and free movement of goods and services (debate)
paragraph: mr president, mr commissioner, the european commission has placed artificial intelligence as one of its priorities for this legislature. as we all know, artificial intelligence has multiple practical applications with enormous potential to improve the functioning of our societies and economies. for this, and for this reason, i am the first in favor of prioritizing it in the european union, but we have to be vigilant. we already lost the boat in digital when, in its anteroom, we were leading the technology market with brands like nokia, who saw how they were left behind for not paying attention and, above all, for not looking from the correct perspective. europe was left off the hook. today we cannot afford the luxury of going back to the same with artificial intelligence. to address this challenge, we must ensure the trust of our consumers. we europeans are not like americans or asians, here we put privacy and transparency before any digital experience. we must ask ourselves: what does the european union want to achieve from artificial intelligence? how does the european union intend to achieve this? and, above all, for what purposes? from here, we ask the european commission to ask these three questions before starting any initiative and to find the correct answers. transparency must be the cornerstone of any initiative related to this technology. without it, consumers will not trust and we will not achieve its development and therefore the competitive advantage that it can give us over our competitors. only if we pay attention, look from the right perspective and are agile will we lead the development of artificial intelligence and create the ecosystem that we europeans ask for and need.

subject_of_business_title: Automated decision-making processes: Ensuring consumer protection, and free movement of goods and services (debate)
paragraph: mr president, machine learning still struggles to perform tasks that we consider easy. for example, a neural network whose goal was to distinguish between dogs and wolves learned to differentiate them, not by what normally distinguishes these two animals, but only by their environment. thus, images with grass were classified as dogs and those with snow as wolves. this example may seem harmless, but it is based on the same learning mechanisms that are implemented on digital platforms and that make decisions automatically. they are the ones who recommend certain products or services to us, make some more visible and hide others. these mechanisms, of course, can also be used with collective benefits, including to improve our public services, if we take some precautions, of an ethical nature, in matters of regulation and in matters of governance. in this resolution we defend, therefore, the need to guarantee greater transparency to the algorithms that feed that learning, in order to provide security in consumer choices and, above all, confidence when they interact with automated systems knowing, for example, whether they are talking to umchatbotu with a human behind this system. we also warn of the impact that these systems can have on product safety, as the commissioner has already mentioned, and on the rules on liability in the event of a defect. and finally, we stress the need for the data, the databases used to train these algorithms, the crucial point, as you mentioned, having the proper quality and being auditable, with clear governance rules to ensure, as much as is technically possible , removing any bias. mr president, commissioner, when it's time for a walk through the forest, we should trust the system that warns us: don't worry, it's a dog and not a wolf approaching.

intervention_header_en: Dita Charanzová, on behalf of the Renew Group
subject_of_business_title: Automated decision-making processes: Ensuring consumer protection, and free movement of goods and services (debate)
paragraph: mr president, i very much welcome the fact that this new parliament will adopt the first resolution on artificial intelligence (ai). i’m sure it is not the last one. automated decision—making is already affecting our lives. it is making our lives easier with new and better services, and making mundane tasks take up less of our time. if done correctly, they also have the possibility to reduce human bias and human errors in the decision—making process. but as with any new technology, there will inevitably be legal and ethical questions raised that we must be aware of. most of these issues can be addressed with the current rules; others may need to be adopted, but we need a measured approach. we need to resist the temptation of over—legislating too quickly for these fast—evolving technologies. this would not only hinder innovation and developments in europe, but also create more problems than it would solve. equally, we must not generalise our approach. the rules governing algorithms should be proportionate to the risk taken in using that algorithm. there is a difference between the algorithm of a power grid and the algorithm in a video game. to conclude, while humans must always be in the driver seat, let’s be guided by our heads and not by illogical fears.

paragraph: mr president, mr commissioner! automatic decision-making systems will literally decide our lives, and even more so those of our children. education and job, home and job, purchase of goods and news are influenced by it. but it is our decision what influence they have, what data the machines use to judge and what they decide - and what not. we want artificial intelligence to really serve everyone, and we can now set the course for this - with a clear yes to artificial intelligence that serves climate protection and sustainability, but also with a clear no if it discriminates against people. because we know that every data set collected in an unequal society has a discriminatory effect. an example: women are currently paid less and do more care work. this fact is included in the data and, if not corrected, will mean that women will continue to be paid poorly or even worse in the future. we must take legal action against such cases of injustice with all determination. in the european union we have the right to safe products and services. but this right is only worth something if we can enforce it. that is why our supervisory authorities need comprehensive powers to check algorithmic systems for their legality. europe now has a unique opportunity to shape a legal framework grounded in our democratic values ​​that could set an example for the world. let us approach this great project with courage.

subject_of_business_title: Automated decision-making processes: Ensuring consumer protection, and free movement of goods and services (debate)
paragraph: mr. president, the rapid development of artificial intelligence and automatic decision-making technologies represents a huge challenge for our society. both from the point of view of law, morality, the future direction of humanity, and also from the point of view of the internal market. we can find the same ills in binary code as in society. services and goods using artificial intelligence and automatic decision-making carry with them the risk of deceiving, discriminating or even harming consumers, e.g. in connection with differentiated prices. thus, artificial intelligence and automatic decision-making may not lead to some kind of flawless society of rationality, but perhaps rather to the entrenchment of the current unjust social state. a state in which greed, deception and bending the law wins. we should therefore work to ensure that consumers are protected from unfair or discriminatory business practices or from the risks associated with professional services using artificial intelligence. automatic decision-making processes should be transparent and subject to supervision by competent authorities, which should have the appropriate means and powers to do so. it is necessary to establish standards and targets, inter alia, in the area of ​​data quality and to eliminate bias in all data sets by introducing safeguards. the european consumer must not be at the mercy of automated decision-making processes. it must be protected and therefore the commission should act.

subject_of_business_title: SMEs and better regulation (debate)
paragraph: mr president, in the european union, small and medium-sized enterprises account for more than 99% of businesses and two thirds of jobs in the private sector. we must therefore encourage their creation and their competitiveness, because they are an essential lever for economic development. this is all the more necessary since the rise of digital technology and artificial intelligence is an opportunity for them to seize. let's help them take advantage of this to enable the most inventive among them to become the economic giants of tomorrow. the european union must therefore restore order to its economic policy. it must facilitate their access to financing by encouraging banks to grant them loans, in particular by granting them loan guarantees. it must also create in their favor the conditions for fair competition within the european market, but also renegotiate the free trade agreements which give too much importance to large companies. finally, it must simplify the allocation of financial aid, the complexity of which often discourages companies that could claim it. in conclusion, i am quite skeptical, commissioner thierry breton, about the commission's real desire to improve things, because your idea of ​​appointing a "mr. sme" seems to me to be a gimmick.

subject_of_business_title: A social Europe in a Digital world (topical debate)
paragraph: madam president, digitization, the implementation of artificial intelligence represents a huge, huge opportunity; we could practically speak of a huge evolutionary leap such as has practically been unparalleled since the industrial revolution. but it is also evident that it entails risks, that it entails changes; and it's also clear that it carries a lot of fears that have to do with control, that have to do with losing jobs, and there's only one way to confront those fears and underscore the enormous opportunity, and thus seize it, which is digital literacy. literacy. which is much more than providing digital skills, which is much more than providing digital tools. it means a humanistic approach to the issue to also democratize the implementation of things like artificial intelligence so that people, not just experts, are aware of what those risks are, those contradictions, those conflicting values, and thus make better decisions. and in some way to be each time a society that goes more hand in hand and in a more integrated way towards the future. so what i ask of the commission and the council is that they make an effort to do so, in a participatory, open process, in which they can underline and unravel this arcane to transform it into something understandable and that can be shared by everyone. .

speaker_polgroup: Group Of The European People's Party (Christian Democrats)
subject_of_business_title: A social Europe in a Digital world (topical debate)
paragraph: i am glad that the president of the european commission, presenting the work plan for the current year, emphasized that digital transformation, in order to be effective and serve europe's economic growth and development, must take into account the interests of all groups of citizens, be fair and beneficial to all. our society is aging, and it is in all of us's interests that older people can remain independent, professionally and socially active for as long as possible. it is worth emphasizing that older people have a huge potential to offer, both in the form of knowledge, professional and life experience, and civic engagement. they are also a very important group of consumers. therefore, when planning the development of digital europe, it should be taken into account that new technological solutions do not contribute to the exclusion of older people, limiting their chances on the labor market, and independence. services, including banking, must be more consumer-friendly and not limit their offer only to people who efficiently use mobile applications. new technologies and artificial intelligence can and should serve to equalize opportunities and compensate for deficits related to age or disability. i also believe that the new skills agenda should include an action plan to develop digital skills tailored to the needs of disadvantaged groups such as the elderly, the long-term unemployed, people with disabilities and early school leavers.

speaker_polgroup: Group Of The European People's Party (Christian Democrats)
subject_of_business_title: EU coordinated action to combat the COVID-19 pandemic and its consequences (continuation of debate)
paragraph: in the context of the current crisis, one of the priorities of the itre committee is to protect europe’s 25 million small and medium enterprises, as well as the sectors of industries most affected, including those sectors that are suffering from disruption of supply chains. accordingly, i reinforce the call for a european horizontal strategy for sme recovery to support them by providing continuous access to finance, reducing red tape and fostering investments in strategic value chains. i express support for the reintegration of supply chains inside the eu and for the proposal for a health autonomy action in strategic areas such as active pharmaceutical ingredients (api). in the same context, i highlight the importance of strengthening the competences, budget and staff of the ecdc and ema, to enable these agencies to efficiently coordinate medical responses during crisis. i am conviced that the eu recovery package will have at its core enough financial resources. finally, the covid-19 crisis proved one more time the necessity to further integrate eu space programs galileo and copernicus. the added value of these systems along with the use of artificial intelligence play a decisive role in combating pandemics and crisis.

speaker_polgroup: Group Of The Progressive Alliance Of Socialists And Democrats In The European Parliament
subject_of_business_title: Presentation of the programme of activities of the German Presidency (debate)
paragraph: mr president, madam president of the commission, dear colleagues in the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen! it is a pleasure for me to address the plenary session of the european parliament at the beginning of the german council presidency. like most of you, i have missed the direct encounters with people, the face-to-face conversations, and for me this is now the first trip abroad since the outbreak of the pandemic, and it leads me consciously and with complete conviction to you, to the heart of european democracy. in these times, in which the european union wants to survive this crisis stronger, the european parliament is needed in these times. the tasks before us are enormous, and they require enormous efforts. they need a parliamentary debate, they need political mediation, they need cultural translations into the different countries and regions. and for that it needs you! it is therefore a special honor for me to present the priorities of the german council presidency to you today. five topics are particularly important to me at this time: our fundamental rights, cohesion, climate protection, digitization and europe's responsibility in the world. these five issues are important because we need to change europe in a sustainable way if we want to protect and preserve europe. only then will europe be able to play its own role in a sovereign and responsible manner, even in a rapidly changing global order. we are all aware that my visit today takes place against the background of the greatest test in the history of the european union. the global coronavirus pandemic has also hit people hard and relentlessly in europe. we have to mourn over a hundred thousand deaths in europe alone. many citizens could not even say goodbye to their loved ones in the last hour due to the strict quarantine rules. this must not be forgotten with all the commitment to a new beginning, with all the commitment to economic recovery: the mourning for the dead, the pain of the impossible farewells. that will stay with us for a long time. our economy has been and is being severely shaken across europe. millions of employees have lost their jobs, and in addition to concerns about health and the health of their families, many citizens are also concerned about their economic existence. they all need our collective support now. in order to break the chains of infection, the most elementary basic rights had to be temporarily restricted. that was a very high price, because generations in europe fought hard for these fundamental rights. human and civil rights are the most valuable asset we have in europe. and they may only be restricted for very important reasons and only for a very short time. a pandemic must never be an excuse to undermine democratic principles. every country in europe remembers its own historical upheavals differently, the different struggles for freedom and the rule of law. and at the same time, it is precisely this achievement of fundamental rights in europe that unites us. for me, who have lived in a system of bondage for thirty-five years of my life, restricting these rights during the pandemic was a decision that i found incredibly difficult. in this historic phase, germany is now taking over the eu council presidency. this task fills me with respect, but also with great passion. because i believe in europe. i believe in europe, not just as a legacy of the past, but as a hope and vision for the future. europe is not just something that has been handed over to us, something destined to oblige us, but europe is something alive that we can shape and change. europe does not deprive us of opportunities for action, but in a globalized world europe gives us some. not without, but only with europe can we preserve our beliefs and freedoms. and for that we need this: more than ever orientation towards fundamental rights, at the same time more than ever mutual support and community cohesion. europe will only remain europe if there are innovative answers to the challenges of climate change and digitization on this basis and if it accepts its responsibility in the world. those are the big challenges, but i'm confident. think of what europe has already passed in terms of trials and conflicts. think, for example, of the failed constitution for europe fifteen years ago or of the economic and financial crises that we fought hard about. or think of the refugee movements five years ago. that was never easy. that always led to injuries. but even the most bitter crises have helped to better understand each other's hardships and needs. we learned together. europe survived all these crises because in the end everyone was aware of what is essential: fundamental rights and cohesion. human and civil rights, the inviolability of human dignity, the freedom for individual personal, political and social development, protection against discrimination and disregard, and last but not least, equal rights - equal rights that are not only claimed but realized -: they form this ethically -political foundation on which europe rests. these are the rights that apply to everyone. they do not apply to some more and others less. they don't always apply to some and only sometimes to others. they seem. that is europe's promise, which we must guarantee: that citizens are really free to live out their religious beliefs, their cultural or political beliefs, that they are allowed to adhere to their respective ideas of happiness or the good life. democracy, including european democracy, thrives on critical public debate. a democracy in which oppositional voices are undesirable, a democracy in which social or cultural or religious diversity is undesirable is not a democracy. the pandemic has shown us all too clearly how precious fundamental rights are, how elementary the freedoms they guarantee are. strong institutions in the european union monitor the protection of these fundamental rights: the european commission, the european court of justice and the european parliament. fundamental rights are the first thing that is close to my heart during this presidency. this must be supported and supplemented by the second principle that defines europe: our cohesion. because europe will only emerge stronger from this crisis if we are willing – despite all our differences – to find common solutions, if we are willing to look at the world through the eyes of others and show understanding for other perspectives. post-crisis europe will be stronger than before if we strengthen community spirit. no one can get through this crisis alone. we are all vulnerable. european solidarity is not just a humane gesture, but a sustainable investment. european cohesion is not just something that is politically imperative, but something that will be worthwhile. and that is also the leitmotif of our council presidency: “together. make europe strong again. i will devote myself to this task with all my passion together with the federal government. but for that i need you! parliament is needed to protect this sense of community in the eu. because you are the mediator of the mutual understanding that we need to reach compromises. they represent almost 450 million citizens in 27 countries. they are the translators of european principles. they explain europe to people and thus mediate between brussels, strasbourg and their home regions. not only do you communicate in 24 languages, you live with this diversity of perspectives and experiences. if not you, who could explain the attitude of other member states to the people of europe? that is why i am asking you, as mediators and mediators of cohesion, for your support during this difficult time. help us to deepen mutual understanding of each other. help us to strengthen europe's cohesion. the top priority of the german council presidency is for europe to come out of the crisis united and stronger. but we don't just want to stabilize europe in the short term – that would not be enough. we also want a europe that inspires hope. we want a europe that faces the challenges of the present with self-confidence and courage. we want a europe that is fit for the future, that asserts its place in the world in an innovative and sustainable way. we want a new beginning for europe. the franco-german initiative of mid-may also follows this conviction. together with french president emmanuel macron, i proposed a european recovery fund of 500 billion euros. i am pleased that the european commission is taking many aspects of this franco-german initiative into account in its proposal for the multiannual financial framework and the recovery programme. discussions are currently taking place on this basis in the european council chaired by charles michel. our common goal is to find an agreement as quickly as possible, because the depth of the economic slump reminds us to hurry. we must not waste any time. only the weakest would suffer. i very much hope that we can reach an agreement this summer. this will still require a great deal of willingness to compromise from all sides – including you. the situation is extraordinary, even unique in the history of the european union. that is why germany has also supported this extraordinary and one-time effort in this magnitude of 500 billion. now it will be important that we also come to an agreement at european level. i am convinced that the social dimension is just as important as the economic one. a socially and economically just europe is crucial for democratic cohesion. it is the best remedy against all those who want to weaken our democracies and call into question what we have in common. for this reason, too, during our council presidency we will focus our attention particularly on young people and children. they are europe's future and have been particularly hard hit by the crisis. we therefore want to promote their development with a european youth work agenda and actively support them on their way into professional life with a strengthened youth guarantee. we must not be naive. in many member states, the opponents of europe are just waiting to use the crisis for their own ends. we must now show all of them where the added value of cooperation in the european union lies. we must show that the return to nationalism means less control, not more, that only acting together as europe protects and strengthens us. it is therefore right and important that the regions particularly affected by the crisis and, above all, the people who live there, can count on our solidarity. it is in our own interest. but at the same time, this always means that the effort that is now necessary for the good of all must not unilaterally place an undue burden on the economically strong member states, that each of us is required to put ourselves in the position of the other. so also consider what individual member states can and cannot achieve – economically, socially and politically. in all of this, i am asking you, as meps, for your support today. i am convinced that everyone is ready for extraordinary solidarity in this crisis. it is germany. coping with the pandemic and its consequences will shape our council presidency. at the same time, we must always keep an eye on the other major challenges of our time that continue to exist. these are issues three, four and five, which will be important for europe. first, climate change. about six months ago, the president of the european commission, ursula von der leyen, presented her climate protection program in this house. she addressed urgent words to you, stressing that europe must act now if our planet is to remain viable. i, too, am convinced that a global solution to climate change is only possible if europe takes on a pioneering role in climate protection. the european commission's strategy for a green deal is therefore an important guideline for us. with your close accompaniment during our council presidency, we want to create the transition to a carbon-neutral economy and society, to a green economy with strong and innovative companies - an economy that protects and strengthens the natural foundations of life and europe's competitiveness for generations to come. it is important to me that we legally establish europe's climate neutrality by 2050. i therefore welcome the european commission's consideration of reducing emissions by 50 to 55 percent by 2030 compared to 1990 levels as an interim step. from this perspective, we will also accompany the work on the european climate protection law. the other major challenge and the fourth point that is particularly important to us during our council presidency is digital change. like climate protection, it requires that we change the way we live and do business in the long term. this triggers fear in many people – fear of losing what is familiar, fear of the pace of change. and that's understandable. but let me be very clear: our commitment to digitization and climate protection does not mean that we are giving up everything that is established and thereby jeopardizing the jobs of millions of europeans. on the contrary, it is about a necessary change in our society that will offer more protection and more sustainability in the long term. because especially in the past few weeks and months, europe's digital dependency on third countries has once again become clear to us. many of us have undoubtedly noticed this in the course of our daily digital communication – be it in technology or in services. it is important that europe becomes digitally sovereign. we want to make progress, especially in key areas such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, but also in building a trustworthy and secure digital infrastructure. but it is also crucial to effectively protect our democracies from cyber threats and disinformation campaigns. because a democracy needs a public in which knowledge and information can be shared, in which citizens can exchange ideas and agree on how they want to live. we are experiencing it right now: the pandemic cannot be fought with lies and disinformation, any more than with hate and hate speech. the limits of fact-denying populism are shown. (applause) in a democracy, you need truth and transparency. this is what distinguishes europe, and germany will campaign for this during its council presidency. and fifth, for europe's responsibility in a globalized world. a look at the map shows that in addition to great britain and the western balkans, europe is surrounded on its external borders by russia, belarus, ukraine, turkey, syria, lebanon, jordan, israel, egypt, libya, tunisia, algeria and morocco, among others . at the same time, we live in a time of global upheaval, in which the force fields are shifting and europe – despite the integration of many member states in the transatlantic alliance – is more on its own. we can and must decide for ourselves who europe wants to be in this rapidly changing world order. more than ever, it depends on whether we are serious about europe, whether we want a europe that preserves its freedom and identity even in times of globalization. in this situation, there is a need for a strong european foreign and security policy. the united kingdom is and will remain an important partner in this. shaping our future relationship will keep us very busy in the coming six months. the progress in the negotiations so far has been – to put it mildly – ​​clear. we have agreed with great britain to speed up these negotiations in order to conclude an agreement in the autumn, which should then be ratified by the end of the year. i will continue to campaign for a good solution. but we should also make provisions for the event that an agreement does not come about after all. during our presidency, we should do everything we can to make progress in three other foreign policy areas, on the one hand at the accession conference, at least with north macedonia, and possibly also with albania - an important step on the way to giving the countries of the western balkans accession prospects - , on the other hand for our relations with our neighboring continent africa and the african union, which we want to deepen at an eu-africa summit with a view to the future. this also includes questions about our migration cooperation. there are more people fleeing than ever before. that is why we have a special responsibility to make progress on an issue that is so central to europe as asylum and migration policy. this is a question that requires a lot of political sensitivity, but we must not look the other way, but must face this humanitarian and political task together. (applause) and last but not least, we will be concerned with our strategic relationship with china, which is characterized by close trade-political ties, but also very different socio-political ideas, first and foremost in respect of human rights and the rule of law. even if the eu-china summit unfortunately cannot take place in september, we want to continue the open dialogue with china. during the german presidency, we also want to continue our reflections on whether or not we want to stick to the principle of unanimity on foreign and security policy issues, and what lessons europe should learn from the coronavirus crisis, for example with a view to how europe's sovereignty in the health sector could be strengthened. we should also have this debate at a conference on the future of europe. which was proposed by the european commission last year and for which you have developed many ideas with your resolutions. i am in favor of a conference that focuses on a few themes, has concrete results and brings together citizens from and in different member states for discussions. i spoke to the president of the european parliament, david sassoli, about this today. mr president, madam president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen! do we want europe? then you need what i talked about today. then you need basic rights and cohesion. then you need answers to climate change and digitization. then europe needs responsibility in the world. then we have to make europe greener, more digital and therefore more innovative and more competitive. because internationally, europe should stand for a legal order, and internationally, europe should stand for innovation and sustainability. that is the vision for europe. let me close with a personal thought. i am a music lover, so it gives me great pleasure that our presidency marks a very special anniversary. in december 2020, the composer of the european anthem, ludwig van beethoven, would have been 250 years old. this ninth symphony fills me again and again and again. every time i listen, i discover something different in the music that hits me and impresses me, just like europe does. it can be rediscovered again and again and it still impresses me. and so let me end today with the wish that the message of this music, the idea of ​​brotherhood and unity, guides us in europe. what message could be more appropriate than this, that this europe is capable of great things if we stand by one another and stick together. (the deputies rise from their seats and applaud the speaker).

must show that the return to nationalism means less control, not more, that only acting together as europe protects and strengthens us. it is therefore right and important that the regions particularly affected by the crisis and, above all, the people who live there, can count on our solidarity. it is in our own interest. but at the same time, this always means that the effort that is now necessary for the good of all must not unilaterally place an undue burden on the economically strong member states, that each of us is required to put ourselves in the position of the other. so also consider what individual member states can and cannot achieve – economically, socially and politically. in all of this, i am asking you, as meps, for your support today. i am convinced that everyone is ready for extraordinary solidarity in this crisis. it is germany. coping with the pandemic and its consequences will shape our council presidency. at the same time, we must always keep an eye on the other major challenges of our time that continue to exist. these are issues three, four and five, which will be important for europe. first, climate change. about six months ago, the president of the european commission, ursula von der leyen, presented her climate protection program in this house. she addressed urgent words to you, stressing that europe must act now if our planet is to remain viable. i, too, am convinced that a global solution to climate change is only possible if europe takes on a pioneering role in climate protection. the european commission's strategy for a green deal is therefore an important guideline for us. with your close accompaniment during our council presidency, we want to create the transition to a carbon-neutral economy and society, to a green economy with strong and innovative companies - an economy that protects and strengthens the natural foundations of life and europe's competitiveness for generations to come. it is important to me that we legally establish europe's climate neutrality by 2050. i therefore welcome the european commission's consideration of reducing emissions by 50 to 55 percent by 2030 compared to 1990 levels as an interim step. from this perspective, we will also accompany the work on the european climate protection law. the other major challenge and the fourth point that is particularly important to us during our council presidency is digital change. like climate protection, it requires that we change the way we live and do business in the long term. this triggers fear in many people – fear of losing what is familiar, fear of the pace of change. and that's understandable. but let me be very clear: our commitment to digitization and climate protection does not mean that we are giving up everything that is established and thereby jeopardizing the jobs of millions of europeans. on the contrary, it is about a necessary change in our society that will offer more protection and more sustainability in the long term. because especially in the past few weeks and months, europe's digital dependency on third countries has once again become clear to us. many of us have undoubtedly noticed this in the course of our daily digital communication – be it in technology or in services. it is important that europe becomes digitally sovereign. we want to make progress, especially in key areas such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, but also in building a trustworthy and secure digital infrastructure. but it is also crucial to effectively protect our democracies from cyber threats and disinformation campaigns. because a democracy needs a public in which knowledge and information can be shared, in which citizens can exchange ideas and agree on how they want to live. we are experiencing it right now: the pandemic cannot be fought with lies and disinformation, any more than with hate and hate speech. the limits of fact-denying populism are shown. (applause) in a democracy, you need truth and transparency. this is what distinguishes europe, and germany will campaign for this during its council presidency. and fifth, for europe's responsibility in a globalized world. a look at the map shows that in addition to great britain and the western balkans, europe is surrounded on its external borders by russia, belarus, ukraine, turkey, syria, lebanon, jordan, israel, egypt, libya, tunisia, algeria and morocco, among others . at the same time, we live in a time of global upheaval, in which the force fields are shifting and europe – despite the integration of many member states in the transatlantic alliance – is more on its own. we can and must decide for ourselves who europe wants to be in this rapidly changing world order. more than ever, it depends on whether we are serious about europe, whether we want a europe that preserves its freedom and identity even in times of globalization. in this situation, there is a need for a strong european foreign and security policy. the united kingdom is and will remain an important partner in this. shaping our future relationship will keep us very busy in the coming six months. the progress in the negotiations so far has been – to put it mildly – ​​clear. we have agreed with great britain to speed up these negotiations in order to conclude an agreement in the autumn, which should then be ratified by the end of the year. i will continue to campaign for a good solution. but we should also make provisions for the event that an agreement does not come about after all. during our presidency, we should do everything we can to make progress in three other foreign policy areas, on the one hand at the accession conference, at least with north macedonia, and possibly also with albania - subject_of_business_title: Chemicals strategy for sustainability (debate)
paragraph: madam president, with this motion for a resolution, the european parliament calls on the commission to proceed with the chemicals strategy for sustainability. chemicals are everywhere. they are in our food, in our water, in our clothes and in our cosmetics. they are in the air that we breathe. in other words, they affect all aspects of our daily life. our first priority is to upgrade the level of protection of the consumer and the environment. for this reason, we are asking for the elimination of risk-hazardous substances and substitutions to safer alternatives when it’s feasible. we call on the commission to take into account the risk posed by endocrine disrupters and the combination effect of different chemicals. commissioner, we are focusing on a very ambitious target by aiming to set the chemical safety standard for the entire world. the european chemicals agency (echa) should support the eu’s international trade policy by defining provisions and fostering regulatory systems built upon eu standards for chemical safety. this would enhance protection beyond the eu borders and extend the level playing field. chemicals are also the industry of industries. a size—based grouping approach will enable the industry, in complementarity with the ‘one substance, one assessment’ principle. this strategy must also grant sufficient time for the industry’s manufacturers in order to deliver safe and performing products and incentivise the eu industrial production and economy. in this regard, the strategy should secure adequate funding to accelerate the development of innovative and safe alternatives. the strategy should also ensure that unnecessary animal tests are avoided, incentivising the development of smart testing strategies and artificial intelligence methods. however, everything is not dependent on this house. everything is not dependent on brussels and on brussels’ political will. that’s why we also have to increase the level of implementation of the existing eu legislation on chemicals, asking the member states to fully implement the current legislative framework in order to provide a safe and sustainable environment as well as a competitive european market. in this strategy, we have three critical allies – the three agencies: echa, the european food safety authority (efsa) and the european medicines agency (ema). firstly we must avoid overlap between these three agencies. secondly, we have to secure their adequate funding by providing additional resources. i would like to conclude with the need for the chemicals strategy for sustainability to be aligned with the two main aspects of the green deal. the first one is green and the second is digital. in this regard, we fully support  echa’s initiative to promote the establishment of a fully-connected and interoperable eu chemical safety database platform to facilitate the seamless sharing of data betweenities and to provide public access to researchers, regulators, industry and the citizens at large. κυρίες και κύριοι συνάδελφοι, επίτροπε, κυρία πρόεδρε, η στρατηγική για τα βιώσιμα χημικά μπορεί να οδηγήσει τη γενιά μας και τα παιδιά μας σε ένα μέλλον με λιγότερα προβλήματα. μπορεί να οδηγήσει τη βιομηχανία σε βιώσιμες λύσεις με πολύ χαμηλότερες επιπτώσεις στο περιβάλλον. αρκεί τα χημικά προϊόντα που εισάγονται από τρίτες χώρες στην πλανήτη, αφορά τη ζωή μας.

subject_of_business_title: State of the Union (topical debate) (continuation of debate)
paragraph: during commission president ursula von der leyen’s state of the european union speech, i was pleased to see ambitious and concrete actions regarding digital and technology policy. more concretely, in three main areas: increasing our industrial data cloud capacities so we can obtain the benefits of innovation and economic growth; a human-cantered approach to artificial intelligence and a new law for eu digital identity; investing in broadband infrastructure and connectivity. i welcome all of these commitments on the side of the commission, as i am a firm believer that we will not be able to achieve any of our ambitious sustainable economy goals without technology. we must work towards identifying the investment streams to cater for future breakthrough technologies to help transform existing industries, e.g. steel and cement, automotive, aviation, and more. we must also strive to identify the ecosystem of start-ups and small smes that can come up with the future clean breakthrough technology solutions and can create european technology leadership. if the european union is to meet our ambitious green goals, maintain our global position and ensure a high living standard for our citizens, we must continue to be at the forefront of technological advancements.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president! dear commissioner, in recent weeks, the documentary "the social dilemma" has consistently been in the top ten most-watched films on netflix. the message of the film or documentary is scary and very powerful at the same time. social media platforms are no longer simple communication tools, but huge profit machines that significantly influence public discourse. they do this by not only deciding which information we are shown, but also deciding which content may be displayed at all and which not - unfortunately often in conflict with the law. however, i do not want the freedom of expression of users in europe to be in the hands of private companies that act as deputy sheriffs and make decisions that only courts are actually allowed to make. if we say that the law should apply online as well as offline, then there must be an end to interference with freedom of expression through overblocking and arbitrary deletion by platforms. the juri report therefore proposes establishing clear procedural rules for the notice and action system when dealing with illegal content. this is important because it creates legal certainty for the platforms on the one hand, but also creates legal certainty for users and respects their fundamental rights. our report also calls for a strong european supervisory authority that can ensure compliance with the rules and, above all, has the necessary enforcement powers to ensure the necessary transparency. an online platform must not be a black box. its actions must be transparent, justified and comprehensible, especially when it makes such important decisions about users' freedom of expression. and that brings me to a point that i'm particularly proud of in our report, that we proposed that we put in place a system that doesn't pre-check uploaded content. in fact, we specifically require the commission that the digital services act must not encourage platforms to use upload filters. even the voluntary use of technical aids by platforms must not result in content being scanned and blocked at the time of upload. and i think that's a huge success after last year's debate and a step towards an internet with no more upload filters. there is also content that is legal, but can still cause great social damage. such content as fake news, disinformation, hate speech and propaganda cannot be subject to the same rules as when dealing with illegal content, since such content is often below the level of taste, but is protected by freedom of expression. and the problem we have with such content is not so much that it exists at all, but that it spreads through the internet like wildfire and is flushed into the timelines of users by platforms because algorithms believe that attention-grabbing content is more important than democratic debate, for example. in this way, platforms can promise their actual customers – not us as users, but the advertisers – that they will provide targeted, personalized advertising in a particularly effective manner. but if algorithms exploit human curiosity for attention-grabbing content for profit reasons and fake news, hate and hate speech are the wrapping paper in which personalized advertising is packaged online, then we as legislators have to step in and take action against this business model. that's why we demand in the report that users have more control over their content. they must decide what content they see and whether they want to see targeted online advertising at all. we must not allow users to be at the mercy of algorithms that erode our shared information base in society and endanger our democracy. if that's the price to pay for enabling silicon valley companies to make more profits from personalized advertising, then the price is clearly too high, and this business model has no place in our digital single market. that is why i am expressly advocating sticking to the text of the committee on legal affairs in tomorrow's vote, despite the split vote that has been requested for advertising. the split vote on paragraph seventeen wants to undermine protection against precisely these harmful business practices - and it is clear to us that this must not happen, the business interests of the advertising industry must not take precedence over the interests of the general public. we are – dear colleagues – not yet leaders in the european union when it comes to the development of ai, but with the discussion we are having here today we are a big step ahead of both china and silicon valley. in europe, artificial intelligence and digital services have to follow our principles, our values ​​and our fundamental rights and not the other way around.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, online services are everywhere, from the way we inform ourselves to the way we keep in touch with friends; from the way we buy books and clothes to the way we travel; from the way we eat to the way we make a date. some people born in a different time, like myself, might want to go back to how it was before, because it seems like a simpler time. but we can’t. we simply cannot put the genie back into the bottle. the online world with digital services, with artificial intelligence – it’s all here to stay. the future will be more digital, not less, and it brings incredible progress that we, as policymakers, should embrace. but... it also brings dangers that we cannot ignore anymore. let us be honest with each other, colleagues. the eu has done more to regulate the online world than any other continent. yet, even here, it is still the wild west! over the past decades, we have not followed up on illegal content and illegal activities online with the same rigour as we have illegal activities offline. we have not achieved any meaningful transparency over how algorithms push content to users on a massive scale. we have not grasped the impact of it on our democracies, our culture and our fundamental rights. instead, we have focused on voluntary cooperation, which is good, but not good enough. not nearly good enough. so as this european parliament discusses these six reports on the digital services act (dsa) and artificial intelligence (ai), i have one overarching message: these digital files matter a great deal more than many people think. we cannot leave this to the private sector without oversight and enforcement. we must keep this in the public debate as a priority and we must regulate, no matter how technical these files are. the difficult challenge before us is to find the balance between digital progress and respect for fundamental rights. as for the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe) dsa report, i’m raising a few issues right now. the value of lawmaking is the real change it effects. if we start off with conflicting regulations and directives that undermine each other instead of complementing each other, we have lost the battle before it starts. we must respect the scope of each digital file. secondly, the fundamentals of the e-commerce directive were great, but its greatest issue was transparency. we must improve and enforce meaningful transparency, and i call for a clear mandate from this parliament. thirdly, we all agree on the importance of notice and action mechanisms to remove illegal content online, but it places the burden almost entirely on users. we therefore should complement notice and action with clear and appropriate obligations to remove illegal content, and it’s the public authorities who should provide the funding to follow up on this. finally, i would like of course personally to thank all the shadows and all my colleagues on the libe dsa report for their excellent cooperation.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, i am going to take the floor on behalf of my colleague and rapporteur for this report, ibán garcía del blanco, who cannot be here today in plenary session and who must be thanked for the immense work he has done. the framework of ethical principles applicable to artificial intelligence is the first legislative initiative report in the artificial intelligence package, produced in parliament. the position of the european parliament that we will approve this week will undoubtedly be essential in future european regulations. the report is the result of long and complex negotiations between all the political groups, which started from very distant positions, and also of the work carried out with the seven parliamentary commissions that have issued opinions. on behalf of the speaker, ibán garcía del blanco, i would like to thank all of you for your work and your commitment to achieve a completely new regulation, which places europe at the forefront of the creation of a regulation that allows technological advances to be transformed into benefits for all. the legislative report contains a resolution proposal with recommendations for the commission and a proposal for a european regulation that establishes the ethical principles applicable to the development, implementation and use of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies in the union. artificial intelligence is presented to us as a technology with the potential to change the world as we know it, it offers great opportunities and carries great risks. our proposal is a balance between, on the one hand, guaranteeing citizens' confidence and security in new technologies and, on the other, supporting innovation in europe. it is a proposal that is respectful of technological neutrality and provides an adequate framework for the future to respond with solvency and responsibility to the rapidity of changes. our report is based on the creation of a regulatory framework of ethical principles that is mandatory for computer programs, algorithms and data included in artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies that are developed, implemented or used in the european union. all technologies operating in europe must respect this anthropocentric perspective. the human dignity, autonomy and security of citizens cannot be called into question and, in the same way, we must guarantee compliance with fundamental rights and the legality of the union. technologies that imply a violation of these principles will not be able to operate in europe, regardless of where they are produced and whether they are supported or in the cloud. secondly, we have agreed on an approach based on the risks they may present. those technologies that may have a significant risk of causing harm or harm ⸺both to citizens and to society as a whole⸺, violating fundamental rights or breaking union laws will be considered high risk. to assess these risks, we have established objective criteria, taking into account the sector, the uses or purposes and the severity of the damages or losses that they may cause. this definition is intended to prevent legal loopholes from occurring. also included is an exhaustive list of sectors and uses that are considered high-risk, such as education, health, employment and worker recruitment, finance and credit granting, automated vehicle transportation, decision-making. public administration or environmental issues. when an application or technology is considered high risk, it must ensure compliance with a series of legal requirements and obligations: guarantee human control, strict security standards, transparency, explainability and responsibility, data reliability, non-discrimination and the elimination of biases in the algorithms and the results of automatic decisions, with very strict privacy guarantees in the case of remote recognition with biometric data and the requirement to apply the most rigorous governance standards. in parliament we also want to guarantee an artificial intelligence that is environmentally sustainable and socially responsible, because an ethical artificial intelligence is democratic, egalitarian, respects workers and intellectual property, cultural diversity and the right to digital illustration. and for this reason we appeal to the member states and the union so that investments in research are directed to those projects that offer a social or environmental benefit. to ensure the democratic development of technologies, both european and national authorities should maintain a dialogue with stakeholders, including civil society, trade unions, setting governance standards and parameters, as well as providing support to smes and companies. emerging. in addition to establishing the principles, we must control compliance with these obligations. our model reinforces european coordination and lists the tasks to be carried out, among others, to establish mandatory guidelines for the assessment of conformity with ethical principles. when they have been tested, a european certificate of conformity with ethical principles is awarded. this guarantee or quality seal will be voluntary for those technologies that are not high risk. each member state will appoint an independent authority in charge of applying these guidelines, granting the european certificate and carrying out continuous supervision of compliance with ethical principles, providing it with sufficient means and resources. the commission should assess which existing or future bodies and agencies can fulfill these tasks. with the rapporteur, in my group we believe that a european agency for artificial intelligence will bring added value to achieve a common goal, shared by all the members of the chamber: to make the european union the world leader in ethical artificial intelligence, which places the human being at the center of their development and guarantees our principles and values.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, since we are talking about artificial intelligence and new technologies, thank you very much to the european parliament and also to the paris office for giving parliamentarians the opportunity to intervene from the offices! thanks also to the president of parliament. madam president, we are talking about artificial intelligence: it is present in our daily life, with social networks obviously, with everyday algorithms, and in our economy too, of course. by 2022, 42% of tasks will be performed by algorithms, compared to 29% today: this is an exponential measure. two out of three companies already use artificial intelligence on a daily basis. two reports have already been presented on responsibility and on ethics. first of all, i would like to thank mr voss for his important report, because it concretely addresses the question of responsibility, as well as the way to regulate the major technologies of the future, such as the autonomous car. it also makes it possible to have a law that is not fragmented and to have legislation and case law that are precisely unified at european level. i would also like to thank mr garcía del blanco, who was also unable to be with you, for his work on the question of ethics, which is first and foremost a question of trust, and in this respect transparency is not an end in itself, it is a tool of trust. i will take the example of image recognition: used by smartphones, recognition is, when it works, a good tool, but there can be deviations, such as when you see a certain number of states police use this technology. my report, madam president, is also an element of protection. after the protection of ethics, after the protection of liability, there is also the protection of innovations, which must be protected via intellectual property. we recommend that the commission review this issue and reset it. never has the planet had so many ideas, since 3.3 million patent applications were filed last year, and it is constantly increasing. the question of this report is who owns the intellectual property right of an intellectual work generated entirely by artificial intelligence. my report, without wishing to discourage human creation, gives a certain number of recommendations. i will name three. we precisely recommend not to recognize the legal personality of an artificial intelligence. we also recommend distinguishing the creation that was assisted by artificial intelligence from a creation that was entirely generated by artificial intelligence. it will also require a big data strategy. i know that margrethe vestager and thierry breton are very sensitive to these questions. this strategy is necessary, we need the big data sets for an artificial intelligence system to develop and also develop ideas. i will end, madam president, with a topical point which is perhaps outside the scope of my report, but which is also part of this joint debate on digital services legislation (dsa). french news also shows us how much we are going to have to think collectively about data regulation: i am talking about the drama we experienced in france with the beheading of a teacher who had been lynched on social networks for weeks. for my part, i think that we must put an end to the self-regulation of social networks and an end to hateful content. we have to get out of the hypocrisy on this question. who can accept that twitter accounts glorify terrorism for weeks without anyone doing anything? in my opinion, no one! who can accept such an outpouring of hate on all networks, on facebook? person. who can accept the public lynching of a teacher who was only doing his job? person. madam president, it is a question of assuming our responsibilities, with our colleagues, with the entire european representation, with the commission and with its support. it is about our values, our european values, our values ​​of democracy. it is a question of regulating social networks and going a little further than the sole question of illegal content by addressing that of harmful content. i think it's a good course of action. thank you very much for allowing us to integrate this reflection from the paris office and from other offices for other colleagues. i will intervene again if necessary in the debate.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, dear vice-president vestager! first of all, my report is now about liability and artificial intelligence, and first of all i would like to thank the shadow rapporteurs very much, because we had a very cooperative spirit here, which has taken us further forward, but which ultimately also sends a strong signal, both to the commission as well as to the member states. digitization as a whole is of course extremely important and a challenge for society and for the economy, but in my opinion it is also about our economic survival. in this context, artificial intelligence is of particular importance and represents a special challenge and is of strategic relevance for our overall economic development. we will only really be able to compete if we actually manage to create a digital single market, because otherwise we would simply be too fragmented compared to other regions of the world. and that's why i think the member states have to look into themselves and sometimes go beyond their competences and say that it's for everyone's good if we also talk about liability under civil law accordingly. you can't just block and then say, that's our competence. no, this is about a digital single market, about the progress of all of us. consequently, we are basically also calling for a regulation in this regard, and we mean it really seriously, especially with regard to this digital single market. what actually led us to do this? we want the individual to also receive compensation as under normal national tort law. but we also want that he doesn't have to explain whether it was the software, the hardware, the wrong operation or wrong algorithms. we just want him to be compensated. we also want to comply with existing liability regulations from the member states. we do not want to prevent artificial intelligence and its system, and we want to move forward in a future-oriented manner. why do we think this is important? we're currently working on developing that. we therefore need a clear view of things, legal certainty, legal clarity, a fully harmonized framework, no fragmentation, in order to rule out the different applications in the internal market. we also want clarity – not only after five to eight years by the highest courts – and we want to fill legal gaps. but that is why there is no over-regulation in the end, so the whole thing is not a revolution, but merely the connection of corresponding risky artificial intelligence systems to what already exists, and we also consider this connection to the existing law to be reasonable. that's why we always have to keep in mind that we, as the legal committee, are currently unable to offer a coherent system because we simply cannot take certain things into account according to internal regulations. the goal here is actually to limit oneself to high-risk applications, because we think that only makes sense to provide appropriate liability. other risk ai systems are subject to the normal legal consequences of liability anyway. for the sake of legal clarity, we want to have a clear list of which ai system falls under this, and we want to act flexibly as legislators so that we can also quickly point out rapid changes by leaving delegated legal acts up to the commission. furthermore, non-pecuniary damages are also addressed, and we ask the commission to examine whether there is a need for harmonization here too.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, madam vice president vestager! the internet was and is a place of freedom, especially in autocratic states, and preserving this freedom is our most important task. but today there is huge concern about this: misinformation is spreading at breathtaking speed, hatred and hate speech are pushing women and minorities out of public digital discourse, and this is also a threat to freedom of expression. but how could this have happened in the last 20 years? today there are a few monopoly-like companies that make the decisive decisions about what people actually see on the internet. that is why we now need new legislation for digital services and new rules for competition. what are the most urgent tasks? we must first put an end to an advertising business model that spies on people and manipulates their behavior. we must also seize this opportunity to put the financing of the quality press back on a secure footing, because we need it so urgently in times of uncertainty. today, three-quarters of digital advertising revenue – in france and germany, for example – goes to google and facebook. secondly, online platforms must disclose the principles according to which they prioritize contributions. we need to shed some light on these platforms, and users need to be able to design their timelines the way they want. thirdly, we need very clear rules for dealing with illegal content, i.e. detailed and binding notice-and-action procedures. transparency and democratic control are also our guiding values ​​for artificial intelligence. artificial intelligence must serve european priorities, and at the moment that is first and foremost the european green deal, because our most urgent task is still climate protection. but when it comes to humans, we need strict rules because we know that artificial intelligence is a good servant but a bad master. we know that artificial intelligence projects problems from the past, such as racism or discrimination against women, into the future and therefore anchors us in the past, and we don't want that. finally, we must also effectively enforce european fundamental rights in the case of artificial intelligence, and that will only work with a european body that can represent the interests of european citizens on an equal footing with global digital companies.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, commissioner, the development of computing, big data and algorithms have made artificial intelligence strategic today. but only people can guarantee that values ​​such as pluralism, solidarity and democracy inoculate us against the errors and abuses that can turn this opportunity into a pandemic of "artificial neglect". we need clear, simple, flexible and common legislation that does not harm the competitiveness of our entrepreneurs in the global market and avoids fragmentation, that controls the generation and operation processes of these tools, detects risks and corrects malfunctions through permanent evaluation and that guarantee a structured participation of the users. this global plan should encourage intense local action, focused on coordinating and learning more about technological capacities, promoting talent and supporting intra-entrepreneurship and the creation of new companies. thus, by contributing knowledge and value to the local industrial system, regions such as the basque country, recently designated as an example of innovation by president von der leyen, should help the union to gain global competitiveness. artificial intelligence needs ethical principles to prevent bias in algorithms, clarify industrial and legal aspects and establish formulas to determine and refine civil liability derived from events in which the influence of artificial intelligence is key. this is a crucial aspect in the field of mobility. from the transport and tourism commission we are committed to artificial intelligence to offer integrated services, better adapted to users and greener. but we warn that without investment in infrastructure so that data is collected and circulated properly, technology will not suffice. the changes that are coming require a holistic vision of urban and interurban transport and innovation and training to consolidate the new trades that smart mobility already demands.

paragraph: madam president! artificial intelligence is everyday life for us. for example, when our music streaming app suggests new songs based on our listening habits. other areas are perhaps less commonplace for most of us, but have the potential to change products, industries, even our entire lives - in medicine, in mobility or in agriculture. the eu has now set itself the goal of creating a uniform set of rules. this is pioneering work, and one simply has to say that it offers a real economic and social opportunity and can become a major locational advantage. there are three points that we must pay particular attention to: firstly, we must promote innovations instead of slowing them down. with any type of regulation, we should remain open to technology and rely on non-bureaucratic rules. second, civil rights are non-negotiable. the protection of fundamental rights is at the top of my agenda. there should be no mass surveillance through automatic facial recognition, nor should there be any obligation to upload filters. third: harmonization in the internal market. we can only increase the chance of artificial intelligence for people and the economy with uniform rules for the entire internal market. this creates the greatest possible legal certainty for companies and consumers. but we don't have to reinvent the wheel for this. in many areas we already have existing regulations, for example on the issue of liability and intellectual property. but we have to take a closer look: in which areas do we perhaps need updates that correspond to the characteristics of artificial intelligence? because our goal must be to set a framework that is smart, open to technology and sustainable and based on ethical principles and fundamental european values. then we can make it, then the european union can make it to the top of the world, to the top of the world in terms of innovation.
