paragraph: madam president! the federal government has just introduced a chat bot that should offer us all orientation in these difficult covid times - an example of artificial intelligence on a small scale. i just tried the bot and realized one thing: normal human-like communication isn't possible outside of cue bingo. a federal government chat bot is of course not a reflection of the breathtaking developments we are facing, but it clearly shows one thing: there can be no ai without humans as creators, but also without humans as end addressees. our strategies for artificial intelligence must be human-centric. and with these reports we are taking the first real step in this direction. we enshrine human responsibility for ai. but we also state: responsibility for people. intelligence may be artificial, but we can only get ahead with real, not artificial, fundamental rights. and that is why we expressly welcome the fact that the report on ethics is not just about philosophizing about abstract ethical principles, but that this is a basis for binding european regulations and for fundamental rights. wherever algorithms cause damage - and we also welcome that in the other report - it should not just be about property that is being protected, but also about personal rights, human dignity and equality. if people don't understand the federal government's chat bot, then the technology has failed. if people are discriminated against by algorithms, then the technology has failed. if artificial intelligence changes human habitat beyond recognition and destroys our climate, then the technology has failed. and this is not an appeal for pessimism, but for optimism about progress. that's the most important thing for us. after all, ai must not be thought of without green accounting. of course we need ai for our green transition, but we can't imagine it without looking at the damage done by artificial intelligence. in frankfurt alone, 20% of the energy costs are caused by data centers. internet consumes more co2 costs in germany than air travel. we have to change that, we have to include that in the green accounting of the ai ​​- that's the only way we can make progress. no ai—technology without fundamental rights and without environmental protection.

paragraph: dear madam president! dear commissioner! creating legal regulations in the area of ​​new technologies is a race against time. innovative systems that elude standard definitions raise great hopes, but also numerous social fears. that is why people, their dignity and rights must always be at the center of digital transformation. it cannot be treated as an unconscious, passive user or – even worse – only as a source of data. the full use of the potential of the digital revolution will be possible only if we properly and transparently define the opportunities and threats brought by the full automation of many areas of our lives. however, no technology is foolproof. it is necessary to change existing regulations in areas such as enforcement of liability for accidents and failures caused by systems based on artificial intelligence. the process of pursuing claims and compensation must be transparent, and the identification of the entity responsible for the payment of compensation must not be a problem. responsibilities in this respect should be distributed in line with the ability of manufacturers, operators and users of systems using artificial intelligence to control risk. this is very important when creating the right insurance products, for example for autonomous vehicles. i am convinced that mr voss's report defines the challenges in this area well and suggests appropriate legal solutions. i hope that the commission will follow our recommendation.

paragraph: mr president, what is, basically, the issue of these various texts which we are discussing this evening? the question is: can we regain control over our digital lives? and is it possible, are we able to invent a european model which is different from that of the united states, where we really notice the pursuit of profit at all costs, and which is also different from the chinese model, where we see although technology is put to the service of mass surveillance so that the dictatorship continues? i believe it is possible, provided you respect a certain number of fundamental principles, to be able to set limits and set a framework. there are at least two points on which, in my opinion, we can go further. the first is facial recognition. i share the doubts that have been expressed by the many human rights organisations, which have warned of the use of artificial intelligence driven cctv, which will disproportionately limit the possibilities of anonymous movement and which is an intolerable invasion of privacy with additional risks, because ai is unable to avoid misidentifications based on gender, age or ethnicity. this is a real problem and we need a european moratorium on video surveillance or, in any case, on facial recognition. the second point is that of consumer protection. we must ensure respect for intellectual property, which is not the case today. platforms like amazon or alibaba market counterfeit products. nearly two-thirds of products today, according to the european consumers bureau, are illegal products. and there, europe must crack down, because it is not up to the platforms to determine what is allowed and what is not. finally, allow me, because i am speaking from paris, to tell you that it is absolutely necessary that the rights of citizens, respect for dignity and respect for human rights be ensured by the platforms, so that we escape this surge of digital hatred which resulted, the day before yesterday in france, in this abominable murder of a teacher who was really being prosecuted by a fatwa. this is also part of the debate on recovering our digital sovereignty and respecting the rights of european citizens.

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteurs for their great work. quite rightly, the starting point is an ethical reflection from which adequate laws must arise. we cannot allow the ethical threshold of ai systems to fall below the human one. artificial intelligence will pose many challenges. one scenario to evaluate concerns its misuse by criminal and terrorist organizations. there is a risk that the software that manages ai will be sabotaged or tampered with. it would be naive to think that cybercrime and computer terrorism will not make a quantum leap with the evolution of artificial intelligence systems. data theft and smuggling, hacking, industrial copyright infringement, sabotage and hostage taking of ai systems. we're not talking science fiction, it's already happened. while we need to protect the patents that manage the systems, it will also be necessary to make these systems accessible to those conducting investigations, such as judges and police forces. it has already been seen in the past how companies that own encryption systems have hindered or even refused access to those investigating terrorist groups and criminal organizations. i therefore want the commission's text on the ethical aspects of ai to strike the right balance between system transparency, citizens' right to privacy, investigative needs for the fight against criminal organizations and copyright protection.

paragraph: chairman, sometimes you are looking for a new charger or a present for your nephew's birthday. and then you come across stuff online for such low prices that you wonder how this can be so cheap. it's almost too good to be true. and that is it! more than two-thirds of products purchased from foreign online marketplaces are illegal or do not meet european safety requirements. their producers are usually not located within the eu, which means that consumers also have to go abroad with their complaint. and now that we work, learn and shop online, e-commerce is booming in europe. that is good, but it is important that people can rely on the quality and safety of their products, especially because our european marketplaces and producers - with a few exceptions - do comply with the rules. i am therefore pleased that the european rules for online services are being revised so that consumers are better protected and our companies are not left behind. this also means that if you are active in the eu, you must have a point of contact in the eu if products or services do not meet european standards. in short, foreign companies must also comply with our rules on our market. due to the corona crisis, we have also seen the potential of new technologies. for example, artificial intelligence helps doctors in the search for a vaccine and in monitoring patients. if we want to use ai on a larger scale, trust of people and companies is crucial for this. clear and transparent rules can help with this. fortunately, ai is not new and is already regulated by various laws. i therefore advocate that when introducing new rules, we ensure that those rules are proportionate to the impact of their application. because a smart thermostat for the heating in the house cannot be compared to an algorithm that spreads fake news via social media. the digital market is pre-eminently an international market and, as far as i'm concerned, our developers should be given the space to realize our european ambitions.

paragraph: mr. president, i am glad that we are discussing a topic that will play such a significant role in shaping the future world and europe - artificial intelligence. the penetration of artificial intelligence systems into manufacturing, services and all sectors of the economy is an integral part of the 4.0 industrial revolution, which will have fundamental and far-reaching effects. ultimately, it will not be a technological change, but a complex cybernetic-physical-social transformation. the development of artificial intelligence will have an impact on the whole society and on all parts of our lives. artificial intelligence is not only a robot, as we might imagine based on karel čapek's play and science fiction, but also software - simply an algorithm, which is often not completely obvious and can cause credibility problems. at the same time, it is absolutely essential that the systems used in europe enjoy the credibility they deserve, also based on compliance with the principle of legality and regulations and ethical principles. it has certainly been heard many times today and will be heard again that we must create a balance - we must have clear rules, but we must not destroy the chances of european companies on the market with excessive restrictions. of course, one can partially agree with this approach. i also prefer that we use european systems and technologies in europe and become imaginary champions in the world market. however, this must never happen at the expense of the protection of european consumers. i believe that it is necessary for artificial intelligence systems to be developed, implemented and used in the european union only if they respect the ethical principles of respect for human autonomy, prevention of harm, fairness and explainability. the fourth industrial revolution does not give us easy challenges, but it is necessary to deal with them as soon as possible. it is true that every opportunity is also a potential threat, and there is really a lot at stake.

paragraph: mr president, today we are debating artificial intelligence, its impacts in the present and the way in which we think it should impact the future of our societies. if it is true that it is pertinent to discuss ethical issues associated with the development and production of artificial intelligence technologies, as well as issues related to civil liability regimes and their need to adapt and adapt to new realities, it is also true that, although the documents contain some positive points, this discussion takes place on an inclined plane, an inclined plane towards capital, where the aim is, in essence, to release producers and manufacturers from responsibility, where ethical issues are more focused on the promotion and development of war-related technologies than on the impacts of artificial intelligence on workers' lives. at a time when so much is said about technological development, digital economy, artificial intelligence, industry 4.0, to impose new attacks on rights and the law of the jungle in working hours, it becomes more important to bring up the debate on the impacts of these important scientific advances and technology in workers' lives. artificial intelligence and robotics contribute to increasing the social productivity of human work. the increase in productivity creates the conditions for a real increase in wages and for a better life, but this potential is permanently called into question in capitalist society in favor of defending and increasing profits. it is in these moments that it is necessary to take sides. we want to place the potential of science and technology at the service of progress and social justice or, on the contrary, at the service of exploitation and profit accumulation for a minority. workers' rights and scientific advances are allies, not enemies, even if the latter are so often used as a tool of pressure and blackmail by employers. artificial intelligence has to be an ally in reducing working hours, combating precariousness and the hardship of work, without this meaning loss of income for workers. it has to be an ally in improving working and living conditions. this is the debate we bring and this is what we are committed to.

paragraph: president! technology helps solve people's everyday problems, fulfills many convenience functions, and carries the possibility of continuous development. at the same time, the power, economic weight and indisputable social impact of the technological giants have attracted the attention of all eu member states. in the european parliament, our task is to ensure the maximum safety of our citizens in the online space, and to guarantee the enforcement of the basic democratic values ​​of transparency and accountability. it is important that what is illegal outside the online space must be considered illegal in the online space as well. to this end, platforms must step up to quickly detect and remove illegal content. we can deal with illegal content only if the member states act in a coordinated and joint manner, taking into account national aspects. digital giants use algorithms to influence our lives on a daily basis, influencing our consumption habits and decisions. therefore, it is important that consumers are informed if a digital service uses artificial intelligence, and that errors caused by this service must also be rectified. if problems are not dealt with, artificial intelligence can lead to wrong decisions, and can influence a decision with false data. one of the greatest challenges of our time is whether we will be able to step out of the digital bubble and dominate technology, or whether we will let technology take control of our lives. in my opinion, we need to create an artificial intelligence ecosystem that serves people's interests, puts people at the center.

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are at the dawn of a major technological revolution, that of artificial intelligence. this revolution will upset our ways of life and we, as legislators, have a duty to foresee and prepare for the world that is coming. some reject technical advances as a whole, they oppose the robotization of our production systems, they imagine taxes on artificial intelligence and robots, taxes that will harm our competitiveness. they are opposed to technologies, such as 5g, necessary for the digitization of our societies. they forget that each innovation that europe sees spinning, each patent that we do not file, each start-up that leaves our continent is a weapon handed over to the hands of our foreign competitors. others imagine a post-human world where man will be one with the machine, where liberalism will have gone so far as to modify the place of man: these apostles of transhumanism must also be fought. but a synthesis between power and ethics is possible. our greek and christian philosophical heritage allows us to navigate the troubled waters of modernity. however, this path can only be ours if we come out of our lethargy. from today, the commission must stand up to the american and chinese artificial intelligence giants, forbid them to collect our data, promote the emergence of european giants, invest in research and development, better remunerate our researchers to avoid their departure from our competitors. however, all this can only be done by abandoning your outdated vision of free and undistorted competition. the opening of access to all markets, equality allowing everyone, without any distinction, to deploy in europe: all this must end. and when you've given it up, you'll need a strategy. you have already tried it with the european data cloud gaia x, last june, but your dogmas have caught up with you and you have scrupulously sabotaged this essential project by opening it up to non-european companies. ladies and gentlemen, let's not miss this ultimate possibility of keeping our european countries in the concert of nations. the survival of our civilization and our independence depends on it.

paragraph: mr president, in this joint debate, we have covered a broad range of subjects, but i will emphasise how much artificial intelligence has an impact on structural inequalities in our societies. we ask for legislation guided by strong ethical principles with the protection of citizens and the environment as a priority. regulation must address racial and gender-based discrimination. such systems need to be subject to constant review and analysis. further research is needed on the way in which algorithms perpetuate harmful biases. when content is considered problematic or dangerous, who decides how it’s removed from platforms? we are particularly concerned that introducing a separate category of legal but harmful context will lead to online censorship. the text does not contain clear enough language on upload filters. even more worrying is the call for an electronic identification scheme that paves the way for master variance. this is a huge issue. most of all, we must reiterate the importance of digital education. only by equipping citizens with facts and enabling them to identify disinformation and misinformation can we make sure that we have an inclusive digital transformation.

paragraph: dear mr. president, the protection of intellectual property is an increasingly important topic at the time of the advent of artificial intelligence. it is obvious that the weight of mental work will constantly increase and its protection will thus become more and more important. until recently, the concept of intellectual property was more or less clear. someone made or created something and if someone else copied it without permission, they broke the law. however, in the age of digital technologies, more and more ambiguity enters this area. we have to answer questions that we would have recently relegated to the world of science fiction. when artificial intelligence will be able to create, who will actually be the owner of the results of this creation? who will be responsible for the autonomous decisions of the machines? and what if artificial intelligence starts creating itself? it may seem premature, but development is moving at a tremendous pace and sooner or later we will be faced with these dilemmas. and then we must already have clear rules and clear legal frameworks. the main principle we must remember is that technology always serves man and society and not the other way around. no matter how complex a machine or program is, it is always just the result of human intelligence and work. therefore, there must always be a person at the end of the decision. just as a person can always decide whether to use artificial intelligence or not, only a person must have the final say in the decision-making process. only in this way can we ensure that artificial intelligence serves us, improves our processes and improves the quality of our services.

paragraph: mister president! dear commissioner, and now dear michael for the german council presidency! i would first like to say a few words about today's debate. it was indeed a very intense, very insightful session. there was also a lot about consumer rights, and there is also an amendment to the report in the committee on legal affairs on this point. i will recommend tomorrow that the amendments in this area be rejected because i believe they should have been included in the imco report and because i also believe that we could very well have discussed these issues in the shadow rapporteur meetings. i would like to say two or three more words about the report "ip rights for artificial intelligence" because i was the shadow rapporteur: i believe that the success of artificial intelligence also depends to a large extent on the availability of data, and it doesn't help, only algorithms to train, we have to ensure that they operate without discrimination, and for that we need data sharing and transfer. and we need that to break up data monopolies and make the digital single market fair for all market participants. this would encourage innovation in europe. however, it is ownership, as well as rules that would have the same effect in practice. at the same time, however, we must ensure that the fruits of the work of human creators are adequately protected. in times when more and more works are created with ai-based tools and when ai is increasingly able to generate works independently without any human input, the value of human work must be recognized, especially in the arts and creative sectors. and one last sentence on the further dsa: we have made it clear here today that we are concerned with freedom of expression on the internet and that we are prepared to fight for it. we look forward to the commission's proposal in december.

paragraph: the types of digital services and the roles of digital service providers have changed significantly since the e-commerce directive was adopted 20 years ago. under the changed circumstances, member states have begun to define online services differently (for example, netzdg in germany, the law regulating illegal online content in france, etc.), and this would inevitably lead to the fragmentation of the european union's single market. therefore, updating the definition of network services is essential. the basic positions of the e-commerce directive should definitely be preserved during the modernization: the principle of limited liability, the principle of the country of location (coo) and the principle of the prohibition of the general obligation to monitor. regulation of digital services should not impose disproportionate new obligations on companies. nor should regulations harm innovation. i am categorically against banning the use of facial recognition systems based on artificial intelligence by the public sector. we must protect people's privacy, but we must not kill innovation. i don't think it's reasonable to ban targeted advertising. as a consumer, i prefer to receive information about goods and services that really interest me, rather than drowning in the noise of plain advertising. it was with a heavy heart that i supported the compromise proposal.

subject_of_business_title: Towards a New Consumer Agenda beyond 2020 (debate)
paragraph: madam president! the covid-19 pandemic has irreversibly moved part of trade, both services and goods, to the digital area. in addition to many advantages, i.e. greater competition between entrepreneurs, faster shopping and access to an enlarged base of suppliers for consumers, this change entails certain risks. this is of particular importance in the context of online platforms or non-common market sellers who are not interested in complying with european union standards. such practices put consumers at risk on the one hand, and european small and medium-sized enterprises on the other. in the face of economic collapse, it is crucial to develop standards that support consumer rights, while not undermining their purchasing power. the challenge for the commission is to update the rules in response to the challenges of the pandemic while not overregulating a recovering market. the revision of the general product safety directive will be one such task. the legal framework developed for breakthrough technologies - such as artificial intelligence - can make it a driving force of the european economy and a tool supporting consumers, or make european economies in the tail of innovative solutions in a dozen or so years. the choice is ours. if only we properly use our predispositions and focus on innovation, the current crisis may be an opportunity for a developmental leap for europe.

subject_of_business_title: Towards a New Consumer Agenda beyond 2020 (debate)
paragraph: madam president, commissioner, the time when we thought that the internet was going to make the market transparent, eliminating information asymmetries, is long gone. we know that the opposite happened, the market power of the big platforms is enormous and is growing by the minute due to the network effect. it's more or less like going “naked” to the market. when we enter an online store, sellers know us better than we do and can therefore exploit our weaknesses and vulnerabilities. if we are looking for sneakers, we are recommended a gym, a personal trainer and maybe even a diet program. we therefore need to “dress up” to regain some power and privacy. consumer data should not be used for purposes other than those for which they were provided, nor should data be collected that is not essential to provide the service sought. commissioner, the digital transition has not only transformed the ways of selling and buying. it also transformed products, which are now confused with services, becoming intelligent and dynamic throughout their life cycle. from the car, which runs by itself, to a simple kitchen machine, from which i order the bolo rei for christmas, instead of going to the pastry shop, as usual. we need to prevent these digital products from becoming obsolete faster and, above all, ensure that the speed at which new products enter the market we are witnessing, european or imported, and their successive updates do not run over our security. the revision of the general product safety directive must, therefore, take into account the conclusions of the imco report, which will be presented today, and, in particular, consider the precautionary principle in relation to innovative products of greater risk, making so that the burden of proof is that they are not dangerous, not the opposite. the slowest innovation, in certain cases, may be the one that deserves the most confidence and the one that lasts without setbacks. or the use of blockchain to ensure better traceability of products, or artificial intelligence to strengthen the capacity of inspection authorities. commissioner, the new agenda, in these and other areas, must serve to give consumers the same weapons available to platforms and other service providers. in short, the new agenda must be a kind of software that updates the current legislation, that makes it bug-free, that makes it suitable for effective consumer protection, in an economy that we want to be sustainable and that we know will be increasingly digital!

subject_of_business_title: Situation of Fundamental Rights in the European Union – Annual Report for the years 2018-2019 (debate)
paragraph: dear mr. president, the annual report for the years 2018-2019, which we are debating today, mentions many areas, such as persistent discrimination, unequal access, the rise of racism and xenophobia, poverty and migration. year after year we find the same thing, not only do people feel that the responsible institutions cannot deal with it, the situation is even getting worse despite the fact that we have legal and financial mechanisms. we must remember, and the current pandemic has confirmed it, that the freedom of an individual ends where the freedom of another begins. for example, wearing a mask is not about whether i like it or not, but about a responsible approach, when by wearing a mask i protect not only myself, but also my surroundings. so we cannot assert our right by denying the right of another. the union cannot have ambitions to be a leader in digitization, artificial intelligence or green agreements if it forgets vulnerable and endangered groups. the poor, elderly and socially excluded cannot be denied the right to a dignified life. no child can be denied the right to education. the union will only fulfill its ambitions if we get rid of the threats of terrorism. people will be safe on the streets, in schools and churches. the union must find a way to prevent disinformation and hoaxes used by extremists. our ambition must be change not only in news writing. here in europe, i must be a leader in respecting the rights of each one of us. these are interconnected areas, complex solutions, and therefore i would like the text of this report to be more balanced.

subject_of_business_title: Pharmaceutical strategy for Europe (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, one of the lessons of the covid-19 pandemic is that we have accelerated the construction of a european health union, and this new pharmaceutical strategy is an opportunity to cement one of the pillars of this new europe for health. with this strategy we must be able to face any pandemic or health threat, put the patient at the centre of all decisions, solve unmet medical needs, ensure access to medicines for all, strengthen the competitiveness of european industry and make europe a world leader in research and health care. we must invest more in the fight against antimicrobial resistance and its rapid spread, which threatens europe with more than 33 000 deaths per year. today there are more than 7,000 rare diseases, 95% of them untreated. we must respond to patients and their families in the face of this great despair. we have a huge gap in pediatric drug research and development, and our children come first. and we cannot allow a european cancer patient to have a difference of between 7% and 90% in access to approved medicines. or you have to wait 90 to 1,000 days for a drug to be marketed after it has been approved. the strategy should also strengthen the competitiveness of the pharmaceutical industry by fostering a stable and robust regulatory system, improving public procurement, speeding up approval procedures without sacrificing safety and facilitating the availability of quality medicines. technological and digital transformation must also be a reality, using artificial intelligence to improve early detection and advance innovative and personalized treatments. and we must boost production in europe and our industrial autonomy so as not to depend on third countries. there are many challenges ahead of us and we must respond to each of them. and to achieve this, the public and private sectors must work together. only in this way will we achieve the balance between innovation, accessibility to it and the sustainability of national health systems. only in this way will we protect one of the great fundamental rights, the health of all, and with great hope for all.

paragraph: madam president! authoritarian governments block or censor social media. platforms delete content after unclear house rules or demands from governments. regardless of whether it is due to politics or general terms and conditions: blocks need algorithms and artificial intelligence to recognize content. when we talk about the democratic regulation of social media, we also have to talk about it: which tools do we allow and who is allowed to hold them? the decision about what is legal and what is illegal should not be left to companies. upload filters and excessive deletion incentives endanger freedom of expression through overblocking. artificial intelligence must give people opportunities instead of taking away their freedom. for this, a legal framework must look at the application, not at the technology itself. the planned regulation of artificial intelligence must protect our fundamental rights. restricting freedom through technological progress would be the greatest step backwards for our society and a dangerous weapon in the hands of authoritarian regimes.

paragraph: madam president, commissioner, my dear colleagues! the dismantling of barriers is one of the greatest achievements in the european union: only the dismantling of our internal borders and the abolition of customs controls have helped the european economy to achieve true greatness. it's about time we transferred this idea to the digital space. that is exactly the goal of the european data strategy - we want to build a schengen for data in europe. data should be able to circulate safely and easily within europe. only if we open our national data silos and link european data and make it usable, which today often still gathers dust unused in public institutions or on the hard drives of medium-sized companies, can we, for example, advance artificial intelligence made in europe. of course, we have to make sure that citizens and companies know exactly what their data is being used for. such a european internal market for data should – precisely as an alternative to the business models of the american data giants – give back control over data to citizens and companies. take health data as an example: a european medical data room could take us years forward in cancer research. for example geo and mobility data: here we can get a lot of useful information for environmental and climate protection. or, for example, all the data generated in agriculture - this also helps our farmers to manage in a more resource-efficient manner. so, we have huge opportunities if we implement the eu data strategy appropriately, and we are all called upon to do that now.

paragraph: madam president, during the first legislature of full validity of the treaty of lisbon and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs of this european parliament - which i have the honor of chairing - consumed a lot of time and energy in exercising its role as legislator of fundamental rights in terms of data protection, approving the general data protection regulation and the directive that protects the data of europeans before the investigation of crimes. and that data protection package finally came into force in 2018, mandating that two years later, in 2020, the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs present an application report. and it does so in a context that could not be more challenging: at a time when the european union is legislating the digital package, artificial intelligence and, at the same time, is facing data protection in controlling the pandemic, in medical research and in the approval of green certificates. and this report has an overall positive assessment. companies, including small and medium-sized ones, have adapted, as well as public administrations, to the new data protection regime. and yet, there are still problems and we detect them. first, abuses of consent by online advertising or "dark employers." secondly, behind-the-scenes abuses of data protection against fundamental rights, such as freedom of expression and communication or freedom of association and collective bargaining. but, thirdly, there are also discrepancies in the way of applying it, because, above all, some countries are failing to provide their data protection agencies with material, technological and personal resources so that they can effectively clamp down on the giants. in the net. and we detect that there are national protection authorities that are not adequately fulfilling their function. therefore, a positive assessment, but at the same time a wake-up call to fully exercise the authority of the data protection authorities to fully enforce the general data protection regulation in the coming years.

paragraph: mr president, the general data protection regulation (gdpr) is not perfect, but it is groundbreaking and aims to set a global standard. in a post-covid world with the rapid development of artificial intelligence and the increased threat of cyber-attacks, a robust and phishing-resistant data legal framework that allows our economy to flourish is vital. the gdpr has the potential to play to the eu's greatest asset: mutual trust, independent oversight and a legal level playing field. but we still need to address persistent inconsistencies, non-compliance and gaps. it's not the time to break all the rules and start over. but it is time to make the regulations work as the legislator intended. we need to consider how we can make gdpr go hand in hand with changing technology. how can we help businesses grow in a digital age? how can we offer smes more guidance and support? and ultimately, how can we better protect our citizens' privacy and data? that's what it should be about!

paragraph: mr. president, dual-use technologies, those that can be used for civil as well as military uses, are almost as old as humanity. if we go back to the paleolithic, we already find flint axes necessary for hunting, but also used for war. technology, by its very nature, is a double-edged sword. on the one hand, it is a tool to generate innovation, new economic opportunities and new jobs. that is why europe must continue to bet on new techniques such as artificial intelligence or quantum computing so as not to lose the global technological race. technology has also been consolidated in recent years as a key instrument to help the state security forces and corps to protect all citizens. but, on the other hand, there are many reasons to control and limit technology transfers and exports of these services outside the european union. if they fall into the wrong hands, these technologies can endanger our own national security or restrict the freedoms and human rights of citizens of third countries. i believe that the report that we are debating today strikes the right balance to continue advancing thanks to technology without seriously endangering rights and freedoms.

building block of that deep integration between countries, between our economies, between our citizens, one of those concrete achievements with which de facto solidarity is built, to quote schuman, a de facto solidarity that arises precisely from these connections, from these exchanges that take place in the common market. compared to the start of negotiations in 2019, the world we knew has completely changed. the covid crisis has highlighted more than ever the importance of a well-integrated, more resilient, functioning internal market in all its aspects. indeed, all the areas financed by the program were on the front line during the crisis and will be even more so during the recovery of our economies. we recall, for example, the blockages of goods and medicines during the first months of the pandemic and how many difficulties this caused in the supply of products. let's move on to the topic of market surveillance: we have seen the numerous withdrawals by our authorities of counterfeit or unsafe goods, perhaps bought online. let's think about the theme of masks. then let's think about consumer protection: how many vulnerable consumers have stumbled upon these sales of unauthorized products and would have needed more support and information on their rights and protection? and then as regards the production of statistics at a european level, let's think about how important the exchange and coordination of information on infections and hospitalizations have been, but also data on the economy in recent months. and yet the safety of the food chain with the prevention and treatment of animal and plant diseases. covid-19 itself is a so-called zoonosis and has made it clear to everyone how fundamental this aspect is for the safety of our citizens. last, but certainly not least, the small and medium-sized enterprises and their workers who have been so seriously affected by the crisis and whose recovery, in a sustainable digital sense, is a fundamental objective on which to focus in the coming months with an eye to the future. all these areas will be funded by this program for the period 2021-2027 and it started as early as january 1st. the program will make it possible to achieve synergies with other programmes, such as digital europe, investeu, horizon europe, the structural funds, but also the funds of the national recovery and resilience plans to strengthen a common leverage effect. in particular, i want to mention the sme window which will be the heir to the old cosme program for the part of the grants to finance competitiveness support, internationalisation, digitalisation and mobility, continuing for example successful projects such as erasmus for young entrepreneurs. of course we would have preferred an even more ambitious budget but we are confident that synergies with other funds will still be able to ensure adequate support. furthermore, as the european parliament we are proud to have fought for the inclusion of business networks and social economy enterprises among the possible beneficiaries of the funds. we then placed the emphasis on environmental sustainability, on vulnerable consumers, we insisted on a specific target with its own budget line on market surveillance. the new challenges of ecommerce, new products, such as connected products and artificial intelligence applications, increasingly highlight how only effective supervision with adequate resources and sufficient staff will be able to face the many and ever new pitfalls that they can endanger the rights and protection of consumers and citizens, thus guaranteeing, instead, products compliant with european rules that circulate freely within the internal market, even when they come from outside the union. finally, i would like to thank the shadow rapporteurs of the internal market committee, my predecessor, rapporteur nicola danti in the last legislature and the draftsmen of the opinion of the industry, agriculture, economic affairs and environment committees. with five commissions involved, it was not obvious to arrive at the negotiation in a unified way; but thanks to the spirit of collaboration always shown, i had the support and confidence to always negotiate on behalf of everyone and so we arrived at a result that was able to meet, i believe, the satisfaction of each of us. i thank the german presidency which made it possible to speed up and conclude the negotiations during its semester with an always constructive attitude. last but certainly not least, let me say, thanks to the commitment of commissioner breton and the officials of dg growth, as well as of course the officials of the directorates-general involved in the negotiations together with it. i think we can all welcome the approval of this program today, which will certainly be a key cog in the engine of european recovery.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Europe programme (debate)
paragraph: mr president, mr commissioner, with this debate the end of the legislative process creating the first european digital programme. today we are fully immersed in a data economy and the stakes are high. we need to greatly improve our digital infrastructure. it must be said that, in this field, we lag behind the united states and china. steps have recently been taken to overcome these shortcomings, for example, the gaia-x program, to develop a digital infrastructure for the cloud. it is a project that is also paving the way towards a european cloud, which is precisely the objective of the recently created european alliance on industrial data and cloud. the digital europe programme, with an endowment of 7.5 billion euros, comes to reinforce these digital capacities through the acquisition of the latest generation supercomputers that the european union does not currently have, but it is also going to invest in strategic projects related to artificial intelligence , cybersecurity and advanced digital skills. in short, the first european digital program will benefit all sectors of our economy, but also research, universities and a host of other sectors. i want to make special mention of smes, because they will be able to count on the digital infrastructure, with supercomputers that allow them to process data through which they can optimize technologies that are so important, such as artificial intelligence.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Europe programme (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, dear colleagues, a digital europe is at the heart of the transformation that the european union has set out to achieve. how to make europe more digital and greener at the same time are the challenges of our generation. the digital europe program will provide strategic funding to meet these challenges in crucial areas: supercomputing, artificial intelligence, cyber security, advanced digital skills and ensuring the widespread use of digital technologies across the economy and society. geopolitically, if we succeed in the transformation today, we will have an advantage in international markets tomorrow. digitization and new technologies will change our lives and allow solutions to many of the challenges we face. for example, our ability to collect, store and process data through artificial intelligence algorithm will increase efficiency and productivity and strengthen the overall competitiveness of the european union. the digital europe program is the first financial instrument of the european union focused on bringing digital technology to citizens, industry, but also to public administrations in the member states, and this will contribute to the digital transformation of the union. for this, we in the european parliament have ensured that digital europe will be synergistic and complementary with the instruments of the new mff, such as the connecting europe facility with the horizon europe programme, and that it will receive adequate funding. with a budget of €7.5 billion and synergies with other financial instruments, it will accelerate the economic recovery and make the digital transformation of the european society and economy, bringing benefits to all.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Europe programme (debate)
paragraph: mr. president, the digital transformation affects all areas of our lives. it permeates all sectors of the economy and provides most of the communication during the pandemic. europe needs to increase its investment in digital technologies if we want to remain competitive and maintain leadership in digitalisation. a successful digital transformation is certainly a condition for a successful economic renewal of europe. we need to improve not only the digital infrastructure, but also invest more in digital skills and ensure a clear and stable legal framework. we use new digital technologies every day. even if we don't realize it, they may sometimes represent a threat, but mostly an opportunity. with the proposed balanced and systematic regulation, it can be an investment with a very quick return. new technologies bring great potential for economic growth, the creation of millions of new jobs, saving lives in the healthcare sector, but also simplifying our way of life. as part of the digital europe program, i appreciate the emphasis on the importance of educating the new generation and retraining the current workforce. investments in cybersecurity and artificial intelligence research and innovation are key areas to work on. but i want to emphasize that when we talk about new technologies, we should always keep in mind the fact that the human being must remain at the center of new technologies and always make the final decision.

subject_of_business_title: Revised industrial strategy for Europe (debate)
paragraph: madam president, madam vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, the pandemic has made clear the fragility of the european industrial system and, consequently, the need to review the industrial strategy presented by the commission a little over a year ago. the centrality of an autonomous and crisis-resilient european industry appears essential today to guarantee our future. some sensitive ecosystems - i am thinking of the health sector but not only - are heavily dependent on third countries for some materials or products which, although numerically not high, risk making our production system vulnerable. we therefore need, firstly, to diversify supply chains, especially for raw materials that we do not have; second, to ensure greater circularity by recovering resources and, finally, to make large investments in research and innovation to create compatible alternatives. this must be accompanied by adequate efforts in the energy field, investing in new energies such as hydrogen to allow the production system, and in particular those industries considered energy-intensive, to keep pace with the climate targets. digital is the other great challenge: with the digital compass we have set the goal for 2030 to reach 75% of companies that use cloud, artificial intelligence and big data and over 90% of smes with a basic level of digitalisation. ambitious goals but the only ones that will allow european industry to remain globally competitive.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector (debate)
paragraph: mr president, madam commissioner, dear colleagues! first of all, even at this late hour, i would like to thank my shadow rapporteurs, the secretariat, and the staff for the good working relationship, cooperation and support. through this cooperation i think a good comprehensive report was possible. we wrote a report on artificial intelligence in the fields of education, culture and audiovisual media. in this report, we call for a clear ethical framework for the use of ai technology in media to ensure people have access to culturally and linguistically diverse content. such a framework should also address the misuse of artificial intelligence to spread fake news and disinformation. we need clear rules for ai technologies so that they protect anti-discrimination, gender equality, pluralism and cultural and linguistic diversity. the use of data that reflects existing inequality or discrimination should be excluded when training artificial intelligence. instead, an inclusive and ethical framework should be developed for the use of datasets that are applied during the deep learning process. there is no doubt that artificial intelligence technologies will encounter us in all areas of life in the future and will certainly also enrich them. however, we must put people at the center of the use of all technology, and especially in the field of education, artificial intelligence technology must be geared towards the people who make the final decision and hold the responsibility in their hands. nevertheless, i think it is wrong to generally classify the education sector as a high-risk sector in the discussion about artificial intelligence. in the education sector in particular, there are all conceivable ways in which ai can be used. some carry higher risks, others far lower. here, however, a clear risk assessment is required and not a generalization of an entire sector in order to be able to classify regulation and security measures depending on the actual current risk. at this point i would also like to remind you of the importance of strengthening digital skills at union level as a prerequisite for the use of artificial intelligence in education and of the need, above all, to train teachers so that they can adapt to the realities of ai-based education can adapt and risks from misuse of technology can be reduced. teachers must always be able to correct decisions made by the ai, such as when grading students. teachers must never be replaced by ai technologies, and especially not in early childhood education. for the cultural and creative sectors, we call for a coherent vision of the use of artificial intelligence at european level and in the member states. algorithm-based content recommendations, especially for video and music streaming services, should not be able to negatively impact cultural and linguistic diversity in the european union. to this end, specific indicators will be developed to assess diversity and ensure that european works are promoted. we want to reduce filter bubbles and enable more transparency for consumers, who can then better understand algorithm decisions. we have fought for decades to establish our values ​​of inclusion, non-discrimination, multilingualism and cultural diversity, which our citizens see as an essential part of european identity. these values ​​must also be reflected in the online world, in which algorithms and artificial intelligence applications are increasingly being used. maximum transparency and the development of high-quality and inclusive data systems for the deployment of deep learning are crucial, as is a clear ethical framework to ensure access to culturally and linguistically diverse content. artificial intelligence is a technology that influences many areas of our lives and is a key driver of digital change. in my opinion, one thing is certain: ultimately, technology must serve people. the human being is the focus and has the responsibility as well as the control and the final decision.

intervention_header_en: Ondřej Kovařík, rapporteur for the opinion of the Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs
subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector (debate)
paragraph: mr president, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe), let me present the main elements from our opinion. primarily, we insist that any use of artificial intelligence in the education, culture and audiovisual sectors must fully respect fundamental rights and freedoms as set down in the treaties. ai can enhance the education process if it’s used wisely, contributing to digital skills which will be so important in the future. about 40% of children today will work in jobs that do not exist yet. i therefore welcome the commission’s intention to update the digital education action plan in this regard. we highlight the need for safeguards in the use of ai for children, who are more vulnerable and therefore deserve particular attention and protection. there must always be the possibility for human intervention to ensure that no bias is found in the systems and there are equal opportunities for all. let me conclude my remarks by calling for an open regulatory framework for artificial intelligence where benefits in the education, audiovisual and cultural sectors are maximised and risks minimised.

intervention_header_en: Ангел Джамбазки, rapporteur for the opinion of the Committee on Legal Affairs
subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner gabriel, artificial intelligence and its application are becoming more and more widespread in various areas of our lives, such as defense for example. we have witnessed a complete shift of activities from our daily lives absent, online. the same thing happened in the field of education, which showed a significant problem that needs to be solved. 42% of the population of the european union lack basic digital skills. i believe that teachers cannot and should not be replaced by machines and programs, at least in the foreseeable future, but funds should be invested in their qualification, in working with artificial intelligence, in interactive teaching. artificial intelligence also plays a role in the spread of fake news. it is important to know how to counter and use it to fight misinformation. i don't think it should be unsupervised and without people, because more than once the use of algorithms by the big social networks and online platforms leads to content being taken down, blocked, which is pure censorship. and this is a serious part, for which i thank and congratulate the rapporteur. however, there is also a very light-hearted part, and i admit, i am impressed, even in this report, when it comes to artificial intelligence, you managed to bring in your favorite topics such as gender propaganda, lgbt and gender equality, etc. even the poor robots of the future will have to deal with this propaganda, which makes their future pretty sad, i think, but what can we do, this is the version we live in.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, thank you first of all to the rapporteur, mrs verheyen, for this very important report. artificial intelligence represents an immense opportunity for players in education, culture and the european audiovisual sector. whether it is more interactive learning devices, particularly linguistic ones, or promoting our heritage, artificial intelligence opens up many possibilities for our performance and our competitiveness. it is therefore essential, as we are asking in this group for this report, to allow everyone equitable and fair access to this digital technology. however, this also obliges us to take up several challenges: first, the strengthening of the digital skills of europeans and the adequate training of teaching staff; then, the structuring of a competitive and attractive cutting-edge research sector for european researchers; finally, the development of an artificial intelligence that is ethical from the design stage and emblematic of our european values, such as cultural diversity, gender equality or freedom of expression and information. europe therefore has its full role to play in meeting these challenges, through its “horizon europe”, “digital europe” and “creative europe” programmes. however, artificial intelligence also has its dark side: deep fakes, which make it possible to fake speeches, or the accelerated dissemination of false information. against these practices, we will have to preserve high-risk areas, such as education, and also fight even more strongly against disinformation. in this respect, we expect a great deal from the framework project proposed by the commission a few weeks ago.

paragraph: mr president, artificial intelligence will bring changes to our societies. however, only if we eliminate the risks will these changes be positive. for instance, ai systems evaluating applications for universities must be considered high risk. imagine that a technology faculty employs such a system and uses graduates’ profiles for machine learning. women are under-represented in technology, so the system may reject applications from women, based on that pattern, and such discrimination is unacceptable. systems with such an impact on people’s lives must be verifiable at every stage of their life cycle by authorities and by civil society. let me remind you that free and open source solutions serve this purpose best. we also need to update curricula so that students are prepared to fully participate in the digital society and to understand how ai systems may influence their decisions, shopping patterns or what they see online. and finally, my group has also been calling for a ban on facial recognition technologies in public space. among other things, they can be easily abused to persecute investigative journalists. and please let me finish by thanking the rapporteur and other shadow rapporteurs for their work on this file.

subject_of_business_title: Digital future of Europe: digital single market and use of AI for European consumers (debate)
paragraph: madam president, shaping the digital future, removing barriers to the functioning of the single market and improving the use of artificial intelligence for consumers – that’s what we’ve been working on for a number of months now and i want to thank my fellow shadows and their offices, and those committees who have contributed opinions to this report. we’ve had strong cooperation, resulting in a balanced report that clearly identifies areas we believe can and should be acted on to improve the functioning of our single market in the digital area. the last 12 months and more have demonstrated to us the value of digitalisation and how it can contribute to bringing people together, to connecting businesses to consumers and connecting business to business. but we can do more to make our single market work better for citizens and businesses, make european smes, micro-businesses and larger companies more competitive, and improve their potential to compete globally. as always, we need to remove unnecessary and unjustified barriers that occur at national level and emphasise the need for a strong european approach that gives certainty to enterprise. european companies should engage with an eu approach to regulation and not have to engage with 27 member state approaches. this certainty will encourage entrepreneurs and others who want to expand and establish themselves in the european union, as they will know that the eu is a place where they can do this. they know for sure what’s expected of them. there will be no barriers, no borders, just a market of 450 million citizens and the support of european regulation that provides legal clarity. european regulation that is trustworthy, fully compliant with fundamental rights, consumer protection rules, data protection rules and is non-discriminatory. these are the traits europe has established for itself and as a leader worldwide, and the traits we also want to embed in our digital rules. of course, this approach is always essential for our public services that support our citizens, regardless of where they reside. as we continue to deal with covid and the fallout from the pandemic, as we face our ambition of implementing the eu green deal, and as we reorganise our healthcare services, digitalisation and emerging technologies such as ai can and will contribute to reaching these objectives. it is really encouraging to see that 25% of the eu rescue fund is going to be earmarked for digital and we must not waiver from that. funding for smes, innovation and tech entrepreneurs is vital if we are to facilitate the development of the eu tech space that we so badly need. if we look at our global competitors in the ai sector, like the united states or china, we can see that more private sector investment is encouraged there than it is here in the european union. yes, we have our investeu, our horizon eu and other programmes, and these are enormously successful, but we must also introduce policies that leverage private sector investment in terms of venture capital or seed capital. we need that private sector investment to ensure that we don’t have scale-ups for sale here in europe, and we don’t have start-ups that will scale up in third countries. we want eu successes. i really welcome the commissioner’s recent proposals to support artificial intelligence through regulation, proposals designed to encourage its use and, importantly, to encourage consumer confidence. ai has enormous potential to address many of the challenges that we face today in the healthcare sector, agriculture and transport, and in developing our smart cities. the list is endless and it does go on, but ai is not without its drawbacks or its risks, such as lack of transparency or traceability, or lack of human oversight, bias decision-making, etc. these need to be addressed through regulation. we already have our data protection rules, privacy rules, non-discrimination rules, but we need to protect consumers as we do with product safety and liability. we need the same protection online as offline, but there are gaps and these need to be addressed. we need to inform consumers on the use of artificial intelligence, where it is being used and when they are engaging with it. consumers have a right to be adequately informed in a timely and easily accessible manner where ai exists and the possible outcomes, how the system is established, is checked, how it can be contested and how it can be corrected. this is a very important position that we have reflected in our report today, because we believe that these criteria are essential if we want to encourage consumer confidence, and they will in turn feed into an ecosystem that allows ai products and technologies to develop. there are risks with artificial intelligence; i don’t deny that. in some areas of operation, the risks will be higher than in others. and we want to see a risk-based regulatory approach that would regulate the highest risk and, as consequence, for lower risks we would have less regulation. there must be the possibility to also prohibit harmful or discriminatory practice. we don’t want to see a binary approach to risk evaluation that could become quickly obsolete, but rather a forward-looking approach that is not application-specific but that gives certainty to developers, certainty to investors and indeed confidence to consumers. so artificial intelligence and the future regulation that we are going to be dealing with in this house are important. it will send out a message that europe can be a leader in this area, as we were with the general data protection regulation. there are gaps. i think it’s another ideal opportunity to lead internally but also can do more to make our single market work better for citizens and businesses, make european smes, micro-businesses and larger companies more competitive, and improve their potential to compete establish themselves in the european union, as they will know that the eu is a place where they can do this. they know for sure what’s expected of them. there will be no barriers, no borders, just a rules, data protection rules and is non-discriminatory. these are the traits europe has established for itself and as a leader worldwide, and the traits we also want to embed in our digital rules. of course, this approach is always essential for our public services that support our citizens, regardless of where they reside. as we continue to deal with covid and the fallout from the pandemic, as we paragraph: madam speaker! mr. commissioner! solutions based on advanced algorithms and using the possibilities of artificial intelligence will play a key role in the modernization of the european transport system. this applies not only to the automation of transport, but also to the creation of intelligent traffic management systems in cities and solutions that improve the safety of vehicles and drivers. without realizing the potential of the digital revolution, it will be virtually impossible to achieve the vision zero goals. one of the key barriers to the practical implementation of ai-based technologies in the transport sector is the lack of clear and consistent rules for determining the division of responsibility in the event of a breakdown or accident. another challenge is to ensure the appropriate level of cybersecurity for communicating vehicles and infrastructure. we must place particular emphasis on this issue in the work on the regulation on artificial intelligence. to create innovative products and services in the transport and tourism sectors, european companies need a huge amount of digital data. we should create a system of incentives for member states to make public data available freely and free of charge, including data falling within the spatial information infrastructure, such as geodetic and cartographic data. only in this way will our potential in the field of artificial intelligence bring real economic benefits.

paragraph: mr. president, the implementation of artificial intelligence brings obvious benefits, but also a number of challenges. artificial intelligence is not another technological revolution, but a mephistophelian temptation – a hostage to which our very existence as a biological species and human society will be held in the future. therefore, economic prospects and competitive pressure are not a sufficient argument for the rapid introduction of new technologies. the huge gap between our human awareness, on the one hand, and the great technological capabilities we already possess, on the other, holds risks. they require real thinking not only in the interests of business and consumers, not only by economists and scientists with a technical profile, but also by humanitarians. automation will lead to the loss of a large number of jobs. digitization creates a new type of discrimination. the success of artificial intelligence presupposes adequate education, guaranteed protection of personal data and, above all, a set of strict ethical principles that protect man and the biosphere.

subject_of_business_title: Digital future of Europe: digital single market and use of AI for European consumers (debate)
paragraph: mr president, mr vice president, dear colleagues! the report by colleague deirdre clune is a successful contribution that shows how the european parliament should make innovations possible through the new ideas of artificial intelligence. we want to promote artificial intelligence in the european union, and this promotion, ladies and gentlemen, can only succeed if we create the right and uniform foundations for it in the internal market. more specifically, this means that we must remove unjustified national barriers. especially new ideas from small and medium-sized companies must not be nipped in the bud with over-regulation. we must therefore be very careful with blanket bans on individual technologies, and this is where the european parliament's report differs very positively from the most recent proposals that we have seen from the european commission. secondly, ladies and gentlemen, we need to create legal clarity for consumers and for companies - we need regulation for the entire internal market. to ensure that robot-assisted operations or software that sorts cvs in a hiring process do not have a discriminatory effect, we need clear and uniform rules that stand up to european standards. and finally, it is also important to create trust in order to ensure that artificial intelligence and its applications work according to our european standards and bring added value in the interest of users and consumers.

paragraph: mr president, dear colleagues, dear commissioner! artificial intelligence conquers the whole of society. artificial intelligence offers great potential for society, the internal market, the environment, can be found in all areas of our world. and that of course gives us a great deal of responsibility for what we want to shape here in this area. algorithms control intelligent vacuum cleaners – we are of course very happy about that – but they also lure consumers to buy online, make decisions in a human resources department or about creditworthiness, yes, they can even be used for automatic mass surveillance. these are then the problems that we have to tackle in order to make it clear that we want to make a policy for the people, in the interests of the people, so that the positive potential of this artificial intelligence can be used, but at the same time the damage that it causes can also actually be limited and prevented. this means that we have to support and protect consumers in particular, because if an algorithm is faulty: how is a normal person - including me - supposed to even recognize where the problems are coming from, what the reason for this problem is? if the application of artificial intelligence can result in fundamental rights, human rights and civil liberties being infringed upon, then we must also resort to prohibition, because we cannot accept such technologies being used. yes, we should use all potential, but yes, we have to ensure that the protection of citizens comes first.

paragraph: mister president! europe's economic future depends crucially on whether we lead the digital transformation or continue to lag behind. i want us to put the eu at the forefront of innovation in the world. above all, this means that we enable the potential of artificial intelligence to develop. first of all, we need fair competition between small and big players, between small and medium-sized companies and tech giants. this works with clear rules that make it easy for the start-up to expand and the requirements are based on size. we must encourage innovation instead of holding it back. this is possible if we remain open to technology and pursue a risk-based approach. because the application and the corresponding risk belong in the focus. with face recognition as an example, we can see that quite nicely, it's handy for unlocking our phone, but biometric surveillance in public spaces is a threat to our civil liberties. as europeans, we must shape digitization with self-confidence, but not alone. independence must not become synonymous with protectionism. on the contrary: if we want to set value-based standards for the digital space, we have to do it together with democratic partners. therefore: let's start an ai alliance with the usa! i work for a digital space in europe where the credo is a desire for progress, where start-ups can become global corporations and where there is fair competition. we now have it in our hands to create a political framework for artificial intelligence in which future wishes can become reality. dear commissioner, dear colleagues, that is our job. this report is a start - but it is only a start, the real work is only beginning.

paragraph: mr. president, mr. vice president schinas, thank you very much for your presence in this important debate. first of all, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs clune, on this important report, which certainly sets the stage for how we should approach artificial intelligence and upcoming technologies. artificial intelligence is one of the technologies that will drive the development of our industry, of our smes, but it is not the only one. it's clear. this will give way to more developed technologies, such as quantum computing, with the potential for multiplied computing power. that is why it is important that the legislation we adopt now is prepared for the technologies that are coming and does not become obsolete in a few years. the advent of technologies such as quantum computing will allow more complex problems to be addressed, in a more agile way than current ones. in addition, it will reduce energy consumption, thus helping to meet the objectives set by the green pact. these technologies have great potential, but they also carry great risks, since they are fed by data. that is why it is very important to ensure the protection and quality of this data, both personal and non-personal. there is a very fine line between the use of personal and non-personal data once it enters the artificial intelligence system. that is why we have to be very rigorous and comply with clear transparency rules that establish red lines, if necessary. for example, we must avoid abusive or discriminatory practices towards consumers and companies caused by the biased use of data in the machine learning process. otherwise, the consumer or smes will not trust these technologies and hinder their development. as vice president vestager has said, in artificial intelligence, trust is a must, not a luxury.

paragraph: mr. chairman, as the shadow reporter of the position of the empl committee, i want to appreciate that my proposals regarding ethical artificial intelligence, the protection of human dignity and rights, but also the overall focus of artificial intelligence on the service of man and his good have received unequivocal support. we use artificial intelligence technology more and more in everyday activities. we mostly perceive them positively as our daily helper. however, there are also areas where even wider use is met with initial distrust, such as in the case of using its influence on the labor market. it is indisputable that many jobs will disappear due to the use of ai. well, that's how it's always been with technological revolutions. our task is to create conditions for using the potential of ai for the creation of new jobs and to ensure retraining and lifelong learning so that people do not lose their jobs. i therefore appeal for clear and sufficient communication between the commission and the member states towards society, not only through the formation of public debate, but above all through the use of effective measures in the education and labor market systems. this is the only way we can fully utilize the potential of this technology without citizens feeling fear or mistrust towards it. it relieves many from work activities that are dangerous or strenuous for a person.

subject_of_business_title: Promoting gender equality in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) education and careers (debate)
paragraph: the underrepresentation of girls and women in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (stem) is a reality that we must reverse. the gender gap that exists in all areas of digital technology is particularly evident in innovative technologies such as artificial intelligence and cyber security. in these sectors, the average presence of women at global level amounts to only 12% and 20% respectively. also, only 18% of information and communication technologies (ict) professionals in europe are women. the participation of more women can potentially add €16 billion to the gdp of the eu economy. stereotypes and the lack of female role models are some of the problems that contribute to the low percentage of women in these sectors. but the need for stem and ict skills is ever-increasing, from healthcare to manufacturing, opening up new and well-paid employment options for everyone. in this context, it is important that women and girls are encouraged to pursue educational and career opportunities in these sectors while removing barriers, combating stereotypes and improving access to finance and investment for female entrepreneurs.
